react-q1.testing: whether you name the programming-model change, not "the virtual DOM".
react-q1.trap: "React is fast because of the virtual DOM."
react-q1.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "React turns UI into a function of state. I describe what the screen should look like for the current data, and React works out how to get the DOM from the old state to the new one."
2 · Mechanism "With hand-written DOM code I own every transition: add this class, remove that node, update this counter in three places. That is where the bugs live, when two places disagree about what the screen should be. In React every change goes through state, and the component is the unit of reuse: markup, behaviour and local state together."
3 · What it costs "The price is an abstraction layer, a runtime in the bundle, and a re-render model I now have to reason about: when things render, and why."
4 · How I've used it "It pays most where many inputs feed one screen: forms, dashboards, a streaming chat."
5 · Adjacent concept "And the natural next question is what happens between setState and the pixel."
Close "State is the single source of truth, and the DOM follows it."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.claim: UI as a function of state
stages.html:
"UI = f(state): I write the target, React computes the transition."

Hand-written DOM React
I write every transition between screens the screen for a given state
Source of truth scattered across DOM nodes and variables state
A new way to change the data more DOM code in more places one more setState
Typical bug two places show different values a re-render I didn't expect

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
Prove it — the same feature, imperative vs declarative:

// Imperative: every transition by hand; easy to forget one
button.onclick = () => { count++; label.textContent = count; if (count > 9) badge.classList.add('hot') }

// Declarative: describe the result; React applies the diff
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0)
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>{count}{count > 9 && <b>hot</b>}</button>
}
  • Imperative: reset, undo or a second button changing count each need matching DOM code. Declarative: every path goes through state.

stages.claim: a model to learn and a runtime to ship
stages.html:
Cost Detail

mental model render vs commit, identity, stale closures, effects
performance traps unnecessary re-renders, effect waterfalls

stages.name: How I've used it

stages.html:
One source of truth:user inputstaterenderevery view that reads it updates
UI State Views derived from it
checkout form fields, errors, submitting inputs, error text, button, summary
dashboard filters, selection charts, table, URL
chat messages, streaming flag transcript, typing indicator, retry button
  • Complex forms, dashboards and streaming chat UIs where many inputs affect one screen: one source of truth, many derived views.

stages.html:
What comes next:setStaterender (pure)commit (DOM)painteffects
  • The follow-up is always "what happens between setState and the pixel?" (Q3).

followUps.question: 🧪 A counter is shown in the header and in a sidebar badge. Imperatively, what goes wrong when you add a reset button?
followUps.html:
The reset handler has to update both places, and forgetting one makes them disagree.

Imperative Declarative
Reset set the header text and the badge text setCount(0)
Risk one place missed none: both read the same state

followUps.question: "React is fast because of the virtual DOM."
followUps.html:
The virtual DOM is a cost React pays so you can write declaratively.

  • Fast enough, not faster than well-written direct DOM code.
  • What you gain is correctness and maintainability at scale (Q6).

followUps.question: What's a component, really?
followUps.html:
A function from props, and its own state, to a description of UI.

props + statecomponent functionelementsReact turns them into DOM

React calls it; you never call it directly.

followUps.question: When would you not use React?
followUps.html:
When the page barely changes, or when React's model is the wrong tool.

Case Better
mostly static content plain HTML or a static site generator
a tiny widget on someone else's page a few lines of DOM code
a performance-extreme canvas drawing directly

followUps.question: For an AI chat product, what does the model buy you?
followUps.html:
Every hard chat feature becomes a state transition.

Feature As state
streaming append to the last message while a flag is set
retry, edit, regenerate replace or truncate the message list
tool-call traces, errors fields on a message

DOM surgery for these is where chat UIs usually break.

dontSay: A tour of features instead of the model.

react-q2.testing: state as a per-render snapshot, and queued updates.
react-q2.trap: answering 3 because "setCount is called three times".
react-q2.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Predict it out loud "It shows 1."
2 · Trace the render "State is a snapshot per render. When the click handler runs, count is the value from the render that created the handler: zero. So all three calls compute zero plus one, and each queues set count to 1. React batches them into one re-render, and the last value wins."
3 · The rule that decides it "The rule is that each render has its own constant, and a plain setState queues a replacement value, not an increment."
4 · Variants that flip it "If I want three increments I use the updater form, set count with c arrow c plus one. Updaters are queued and each receives the result of the previous one, so they compute 1, 2, 3."
5 · The production version "In production this is the lost-update bug: a like button or a quantity stepper that drops clicks, because a handler or an async callback computed from an old snapshot."
Close "If the next state depends on the previous state, use the updater."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  const handleClick = () => {
    setCount(count + 1);
    setCount(count + 1);
    setCount(count + 1);
  };
  return <button onClick={handleClick}>{count}</button>;
}
  • A: 3 · B: 1 · C: 0 · D: 2

stages.name: Trace the render
stages.claim: three writes of the same value
stages.html:
Call count read Queued update
1 0 set to 1
2 0 set to 1
3 0 set to 1
re-render — count = 1

Prove it:

// click once, then read the button
// → "1"   (React 19.3, jsdom harness)
// with setCount(c => c + 1) ×3
// → "3"

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.html:
Call Queues Applied to the pending state
setCount(value) "replace with value" ignores what was pending
setCount(fn) "apply fn" receives the result of the previous update
Where count comes from: render N creates const countthe handler closes over itevery line in that handler sees the same value
  • Each render has its own count constant; handlers close over it (a JavaScript closure, not React magic).
  • setX(value) queues a replacement; setX(fn) queues a function applied to the pending state.

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.html:
Variant Result
three setCount(c => c + 1) 3
setCount(count + 1) then setCount(c => c + 1) 2
setCount(c => c + 1) then setCount(count + 1) 1
console.log(count) after the calls logs 0 (snapshot)

stages.name: The production version
stages.html:
Where it shows up Symptom Fix
like or quantity buttons, clicked fast some clicks don't count updater form
an async callback using count it writes an old value back updater form, or read from a ref
several fields that change together they drift apart useReducer
  • Likes, quantity steppers, "load more" counters: rapid clicks or async callbacks using the snapshot lose updates. Updater form everywhere the next value depends on the previous one; useReducer when several fields change together.

followUps.question: setCount(count + 1); setCount(c => c + 1) — what renders?
followUps.html:
2.

Call Pending state after
setCount(count + 1) with count = 0 1
setCount(c => c + 1) 2

followUps.question: "setState is async, that's why."
followUps.html:
Imprecise: the real reason is that count is a constant of the current render.

  • Even a synchronous update couldn't change that variable inside the running handler.
  • "Async" describes scheduling; the snapshot explains the arithmetic.

followUps.question: How many re-renders does one click cause?
followUps.html:
One.

three updates in one handlerbatchedone renderone commit

Since React 18 this batching also applies in timeouts and promises.

followUps.question: When is setCount(count + 1) fine?
followUps.html:
When it is the only update and nothing asynchronous sits between reading and writing.

Situation Form
set to a known value (setOpen(true)) plain value
next depends on previous updater

followUps.question: A cart quantity stepper loses clicks under a slow network. Why and fix?
followUps.html:
Handlers or async callbacks compute from a stale snapshot.

  • Local state: updater form.
  • Server: send the intended delta or final value with an idempotency key.
  • Then reconcile with the server's response (Q26).

react-q3.testing: schedule → render (pure, interruptible) → commit (atomic) → layout effects → paint → passive effects.
react-q3.trap: "React updates the DOM when you call setState."
react-q3.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "Calling setState doesn't touch the DOM. It enqueues an update on that component with a priority, a click is urgent and a transition is not, and schedules work."
2 · What React does "Then the render phase: React calls the component functions that need re-rendering, from the updated component down its subtree, and compares the new elements with the previous ones. This phase must be pure, because in concurrent rendering React can pause it, throw it away, or run it twice in development. Then the commit phase, which is synchronous: React applies all DOM mutations at once, attaches refs, and runs layout effects before the browser paints."
3 · Prove it "The log order proves it: render, then layout effect, then effect."
4 · Where it bites "It bites when render has side effects, when render or a layout effect is heavy, or when I measure the DOM in a passive effect and get a flicker."
5 · What changed by version "Since 18 the render phase is interruptible and batching is automatic everywhere."
Close "Keep render cheap and pure, keep layout effects rare, and put side effects in useEffect."

stages.name: The one-line claim
What React does
stages.html:
Phase Work Can be interrupted?
schedule queue update with a lane (priority), batch —
render call components, reconcile children yes (concurrent)
commit mutate DOM, set refs, layout effects no
paint browser —
passive effects useEffect callbacks and cleanups runs after paint

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
function Demo() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0)
  console.log('render', n)
  useLayoutEffect(() => console.log('layout effect', n))
  useEffect(() => console.log('effect', n))
  return <button onClick={() => setN(1)}>{n}</button>
}
// after one click (no StrictMode):
// → render 1 · layout effect 1 · effect 1     (React 19.3, jsdom harness)

Development StrictMode adds a second render and effect pass on mount (Q12).

stages.name: Where it bites
stages.claim: impure render and heavy layout effects
stages.html:
Mistake Effect
side effects in render duplicated or lost in concurrent/StrictMode renders
heavy work in render slow commits, poor INP
measuring DOM in useEffect a visible flicker (use layout effect)
heavy useLayoutEffect blocks paint

stages.name: What changed by version
stages.html:
Version Change to this pipeline
17 and earlier render is synchronous; batching only inside React event handlers
18 interruptible (concurrent) render; automatic batching everywhere; transitions
19 Actions and use; the optional React Compiler removes some render work
  • 18: concurrent rendering (interruptible render phase), automatic batching everywhere, transitions.
  • 19: Actions, use, and the React Compiler (optional) reducing re-render work.

followUps.question: You call setN(1) and then console.log(ref.current.textContent) in the same handler. What does it log?
followUps.html:
The old value: the DOM hasn't been committed yet.

handler: setN(1)read DOM (still 0)handler endsrendercommit (now 1)

Read it in an effect after commit. flushSync forces a synchronous commit and is rarely justified.

followUps.question: "The virtual DOM diff is what makes updates expensive."
followUps.html:
Usually the cost is re-running component functions, not the diff.

Where time goes Typical share
calling components and what they compute most of it
diffing elements small
DOM mutations in commit large only for big DOM changes

Profile before deciding.

followUps.question: Why must render be pure?
followUps.html:
Because React may run it more than once, or throw the result away.

  • Concurrent rendering: a render can be paused and restarted.
  • StrictMode in development: renders twice on purpose.
  • Suspense: a render can be abandoned.

A side effect in render would run the wrong number of times.

followUps.question: What does a "lane" mean?
followUps.html:
A priority bucket for updates.

Lane Example Treatment
sync / default a click, typing rendered first
transition filtering a big list can be interrupted by urgent work

followUps.question: INP is poor on a filter page. How does this model guide you?
followUps.html:
It tells me which phase to measure, and each phase has its own fix.

Slow phase Cause Fix
render too many components, heavy calculation move state down, memoise, transitions
commit a huge DOM change virtualise
effects heavy work after paint defer or split it

react-q4.testing: the two heuristics (type and key) and identity-based state preservation.
react-q4.trap: "keys are for performance" or "keys just silence a warning".
react-q4.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "Reconciliation is how React turns a new element tree into DOM updates. A general tree diff is far too expensive, so React uses two heuristics that make it linear."
2 · What React does "First, type. If the element at a position has a different type, a div becomes a span, React throws away the old subtree with all its state and mounts a new one. Same type: it keeps the instance and updates props. Second, keys. Among siblings React matches old and new children by key, not by position, so when an item moves, its state, DOM and focus move with it."
3 · Prove it "A small test shows it: delete the first row, and with index keys the inputs keep the old rows' values; with ID keys each input stays with its item."
4 · Where it bites "It bites with index keys on lists that change, with random keys that remount everything, and when the same component type at the same slot keeps state I expected to reset."
5 · What changed by version "These rules have been stable since React 16."
Close "A key is identity: stable and unique among siblings, usually a database ID."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: type decides remount, key is identity
stages.html:
"Same type at the same slot → update; different type → remount; in lists, the key is the slot."

Deciding what to do with one slot:same positionsame type?unmount, mount new
If the type matches:same key?keep the instance, update props

stages.name: What React does
stages.html:
Situation React's action
same type, same position keep instance, update props
different type unmount subtree (state lost), mount new
list children with keys match by key; move, insert, remove
list children without keys match by index (warning)
key changes on one element treated as a new instance: remount

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: state follows the key, not the position
stages.html:
function Row({ label }) { return <li><span>{label}</span><input defaultValue={label + '-note'} /></li> }
function List({ items, byIndex }) { return <ul>{items.map((it, i) => <Row key={byIndex ? i : it} label={it} />)}</ul> }
// render ['a','b','c'], then ['b','c'] (delete 'a'); read label:input per row
// → key=index  b:a-note c:b-note     (inputs kept their old rows' values)
// → key=id     b:b-note c:c-note     (React 19.3, jsdom harness)

stages.name: Where it bites
stages.html:
Mistake What React does Symptom
index keys on an editable or reorderable list reuses the instance at each position inputs and state show another row's data
key={Math.random()} every render looks like all-new children everything remounts: state and focus lost, slow
same type swapped at the same slot keeps the instance state you expected to reset is still there
  • Index keys on editable or reorderable lists (Q5).
  • Random keys (Math.random()) → every render remounts everything: lost state, slow.
  • Same component type swapped conditionally at the same slot keeps state you expected to reset (Q30 — fix with a key).

stages.name: What changed by version
stages.html:
Version Identity rules
16 (Fiber) onward the two heuristics as described
18, 19 unchanged
React Compiler doesn't change them
  • The heuristics have been stable since React 16 (Fiber). React 19 adds nothing new here; the React Compiler doesn't change identity rules.

followUps.question: {isAdmin ? <Panel /> : <Panel />} — does toggling isAdmin reset Panel's state?
followUps.html:
No: same type at the same position, so React keeps the instance.

Code Toggle resets state?
{isAdmin ? <Panel /> : <Panel />} no
with key={isAdmin ? 'admin' : 'user'} yes

followUps.question: "Keys are a performance optimisation."
followUps.html:
They are about correctness first: which instance keeps which state.

  • Correctness: state, focus and DOM follow the right item.
  • Performance follows from it: React moves a node instead of re-creating it.

followUps.question: Why not do a full tree diff?
followUps.html:
Because the optimal algorithm is far too slow.

optimal tree edit distance   about O(n³)
React's two heuristics       O(n)        ← works because UIs rarely move subtrees between levels

followUps.question: Do keys need to be globally unique?
followUps.html:
No, only among siblings in the same list.

Scope Requirement
siblings in one list unique and stable
different lists or levels may repeat

followUps.question: Where have you used a key deliberately?
followUps.html:
To reset a form or editor when the selected record changes.

key={recordId}new recordReact unmounts the old editormounts a fresh one with clean state

It replaces an effect that clears state by hand (Q30).

react-q5.testing: index keys encode position, not identity, so state stays at the position.
react-q5.trap: blaming the form library or the state update.
react-q5.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Read the symptom "Labels are right and inputs are wrong, which tells me props updated and something not driven by props stayed behind."
2 · Measure before guessing "I'd reproduce it by deleting the first row and comparing each label with its input. The mismatch shifts by exactly one row."
3 · Rank the suspects "The first suspect is identity. Index keys tell React that a row's identity is its position. After the delete, the item that was at index one is now at index zero, so React matches it with the component that belonged to the deleted row and just passes new props."
4 · Confirm "A minimal test confirms it: with index keys the inputs keep the old values; with ID keys they follow their items. Anything not driven by props stays at the position: useState inside the row, and uncontrolled DOM state like typed text and focus."
5 · Fix "The fix is a stable key from the data, the item's ID. If items have none, I generate one when the item is created, not during render."
6 · Guard against the next one "And I'd add the lint rule against index keys and a test that deletes a middle row."
Close "Index keys encode position; state stays at the position, so the key must be the item's identity."

stages.name: Read the symptom
stages.html:
Part of a row Driven by After deleting row 1
label text props correct
useState inside the row the component instance belongs to the old row at that position
typed input value, focus, scroll the DOM node belongs to the old row at that position
  • Prop-driven text updates; component state and DOM state (uncontrolled inputs, focus) don't.

stages.name: Measure before guessing
stages.claim: reproduce with a delete in the middle
stages.html:
Reproduce:render three rowstype in each inputdelete the firstcompare label and input per row
Position Label after delete Input shows
0 b what was typed for a
1 c what was typed for b
  • Delete the first row and compare each row's label with its input. The mismatch shifts by one row.

stages.name: Rank the suspects
stages.html:
Suspect Tell
index keys mismatch appears exactly after insert/delete/reorder
missing keys (defaults to index) same, with a console warning
random keys inputs lose focus and reset every render
state stored per position in a parent array same symptom, data-level

stages.name: Confirm
stages.html:
Prove it:

function Row({ label }) { return <li><span>{label}</span><input defaultValue={label + '-note'} /></li> }
function List({ items, byIndex }) { return <ul>{items.map((it, i) => <Row key={byIndex ? i : it} label={it} />)}</ul> }
// render ['a','b','c'], then ['b','c']
// → key=index  b:a-note c:b-note
// → key=id     b:b-note c:c-note     (React 19.3, jsdom harness)

stages.name: Fix
stages.html:
Wrong:key={index}deleteinstances stay at positionsprops shift under them
Right:key={item.id}deletethat item's instance is removedthe others move up
  • key={item.id}; for client-created rows, assign crypto.randomUUID() when the row is created and store it with the item.
  • Prefer controlled inputs whose value lives with the item, so data and UI can't drift.

stages.name: Guard against the next one
stages.claim: a lint rule and a delete test
stages.html:
Guard Catches
react/no-array-index-key lint rule the pattern at review time
a test that deletes a middle row and asserts each input the behaviour, whatever the cause
per-row state keyed by ID in the parent, not by index the data-level version of the same bug
  • Lint rule react/no-array-index-key; a test that deletes a middle row and asserts each input's value.

followUps.question: 🧪 Same list, but rows only display text (no inputs, no state). Any visible bug with index keys?
followUps.html:
No visible bug: every row is fully driven by props.

Row content Index keys
text only correct; every row re-renders, so slower on big lists
inputs or local state wrong values after insert, delete or reorder

followUps.question: "Index keys are fine because the warning goes away."
followUps.html:
The warning disappears; the bug doesn't.

  • Safe only for static lists that never reorder, insert or delete.
  • Otherwise it is the same as having no key.

followUps.question: Why is key={Math.random()} worse?
followUps.html:
Every render produces new keys, so every row remounts.

renderall keys newunmount every rowmount every rowstate and focus lost

followUps.question: Does React.memo help here?
followUps.html:
No. Memo skips re-renders; it doesn't change which instance matches which item.

Tool Affects
key identity
memo whether a matched instance re-renders

followUps.question: A drag-and-drop list of editable cards has this bug in production. How do you fix it safely?
followUps.html:
Switch to stable IDs, and look for the same bug in the data.

  • Keys: the card's ID.
  • Parent state stored by index (expanded rows, drafts): move to maps keyed by ID.
  • Regression tests for reorder and delete.

react-q6.testing: honesty about overhead, and knowing what the virtual DOM is actually for.
react-q6.trap: "Yes, the virtual DOM makes React fast."
react-q6.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "No. The virtual DOM is extra work on top of the DOM updates you'd do anyway."
2 · Where direct DOM wins "For any single update, optimal direct DOM code is at least as fast. React builds a description of the UI, compares it with the previous one, and then applies the same DOM changes a careful hand-written update would apply."
3 · Where React's model wins "What the virtual DOM buys is a declarative model that is fast enough by default. I describe the whole screen for the current state, and React batches and minimises the DOM writes, so I don't hand-optimise every transition."
4 · The deciding question "The practical question is where the time goes: in running components, or in the DOM."
5 · What I'd say "So I'd say: React for application UI, with escape hatches for hot paths. It is also why Svelte and Solid compile to direct updates, and why React's own compiler is about doing less render work, not a faster diff."
Close "It's overhead paid for a programming model, not a performance feature."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: raw speed vs a fast-enough declarative model
stages.html:
"The virtual DOM is overhead paid for a programming model, not a performance feature."

Direct DOM React
Work per update the DOM write run components, diff, then the same DOM write
Who finds what changed you React
Speed fastest possible, if written well fast enough by default
Cost at scale every transition written and kept correct by hand a runtime and a render model

stages.name: Where direct DOM wins
stages.html:
Case Why direct wins
one text node changes one write, no component run, no diff
very frequent updates (a canvas-like visual, tokens streaming into a huge list) per-update overhead adds up
  • One text node change: direct write is one operation; React re-runs the component, diffs, then writes.
  • High-frequency updates (60 fps canvas-like visuals, token streams into a huge list) can need direct DOM or refs.

stages.name: Where React's model wins
stages.html:
Prove it — the work per update (conceptual):

Direct:  compute change → 1 DOM write
React:   call component(s) → build elements → diff → same DOM write(s)
         + automatic batching of many state changes into one commit
  • Across a large app, batching and avoiding stale DOM state usually matter more than per-update overhead.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
Profiler shows Bottleneck Fix
long component render times render work move state down, memoise, compiler
long commits, big DOM DOM work virtualise, render less
  • Profile: if component render time dominates, reduce renders (state placement, memo, compiler); if DOM work dominates, reduce DOM (virtualisation).

stages.name: What I'd say
stages.html:
In a React app:React for the applicationprofilea hot path?isolate it in one component with a ref or a canvas
  • React for app UIs; escape hatches (refs, direct DOM, canvas) for hot paths like streaming visualisations.

followUps.question: 🧪 A component re-renders but produces an identical element tree. How many DOM writes happen?
followUps.html:
Zero.

re-rendersame elementsdiff finds nothingno DOM write

The render and the diff were still paid for, which is why unnecessary re-renders cost CPU.

followUps.question: "Virtual DOM is why React is fast."
followUps.html:
It is why React is fast enough while being declarative.

Approach Per-update cost
direct DOM, compiled frameworks lowest
virtual DOM a little more, for a simpler model

followUps.question: How do Svelte and Solid avoid it?
followUps.html:
They compile components into code that updates exactly the affected DOM nodes.

state changesonly the expressions that read it re-runthose nodes are written

No tree diff is needed.

followUps.question: Where does React spend time in practice?
followUps.html:
Mostly in running component functions and effects, not in the diff.

  • The Profiler's render timings show which components.
  • Commit time is large only when a lot of DOM changes.

followUps.question: Would you drop to direct DOM in a React app?
followUps.html:
For hot paths only, isolated and measured.

Hot path Escape hatch
streaming token display append through a ref
charts, canvases draw directly

React keeps the rest of the screen.

react-q7.testing: hooks are matched by call order, not by name.
react-q7.trap: reciting "the rules of hooks say so".
react-q7.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "Because React identifies hooks by the order they are called, not by name."
2 · What React does "Each component instance has a list of hook states. On every render the first hook call reads the first node, the second reads the second, and so on. Nothing in a useState call says which state it is; its position is its identity. If a condition skips a hook on one render, every hook after it reads the wrong node."
3 · Prove it "React catches some cases: if fewer or more hooks ran than last time, it throws rendered fewer hooks than expected."
4 · Where it bites "But not all, so early returns before hooks and hooks in loops can lose state silently. That is why the ESLint rule, not the runtime, is the real guard."
5 · What changed by version "The one exception is use in React 19, which isn't slot-based and can be called conditionally."
Close "Call hooks unconditionally at the top, and put the condition inside the hook, in the output, or in a child component."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
"Hook state is stored in call order; skipping a call shifts every later hook onto someone else's state."

Call № Render 1 Render 2, first hook skipped

2 useEffect → slot 1 useState(0) → slot 1 (an effect slot)

react-q8.testing: stale closures in effects, and fixing them without lying to the dependency array.
react-q8.trap: "just add count to the dependency array" without seeing the cost.
react-q8.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Predict it out loud "B: the interval callback closed over count from the first render."
2 · Trace the render "The effect runs once, because of the empty dependency array, and creates an interval whose callback captured count equal to zero. Every tick it calls set count with zero plus one. The first tick changes 0 to 1; every later tick sets 1 again, which React ignores."
3 · The rule that decides it "The rule is that an effect sees the props and state of the render it was created in, and an empty array means it is never re-created."
4 · Variants that flip it "The fix is the updater form, set count with c arrow c plus one. Then the effect doesn't read count at all, the empty array is honest, and one interval runs for the component's lifetime. Adding count to the dependencies also works, but it tears down and recreates the interval every second, which drifts the timing."
5 · The production version "In production this is a poller sending the filters from mount time, or a socket handler using old props."
Close "Don't read stale values in a long-lived effect: use an updater, a ref, or an effect event."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
function Timer() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000);
    return () => clearInterval(id);
  }, []);
  return <h1>{count}</h1>;
}
  • A: clearInterval runs too early · B: the interval closes over count from the first render · C: setCount is not batched inside setInterval · D: the empty dep array is illegal here

Tick count in closure Update Screen

// with setCount(c => c + 1)
// → keeps counting

followUps.html:
Each change clears and recreates the interval.

  • Timing drifts: every tick restarts the timer.
  • Churn: an effect cleanup and setup on every update.

followUps.question: What is useEffectEvent?
followUps.html:
A hook for logic called from effects that should see the latest values without re-running the effect.

In the dependency array Sees latest props and state
a normal callback yes yes, by re-running the effect
an effect event no yes

followUps.question: Where does this show up in production?
followUps.html:
In any long-lived subscription that reads props or state.

  • A live dashboard poller that keeps requesting the filters selected at mount.
  • A chat socket handler that appends to an old message list.
  • Fix: re-subscribe when the inputs change, and use updaters for local state.

react-q9.testing: dependency arrays compare by reference, and the fix belongs where the object is created.
react-q9.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Read the symptom "An effect that fires on every render with a dependency array means a dependency is changing every render, at least by reference."
2 · Measure before guessing "React compares dependencies with Object.is, which for objects means the same reference. A small test shows it: an inline object makes the effect run four times in four renders; the memoised one runs once."
3 · Rank the suspects "So the suspects are things created during render: an object or array literal here, an object built in a parent and passed down, a derived array, or a function."
4 · Confirm "I'd confirm by comparing the previous and current value with a ref, or by looking at which props changed in DevTools."
5 · Fix "The fix belongs where the object is created. Depend on the primitive fields the effect uses, or memoise the object there, or keep filters in state or the URL so the reference only changes when the user changes them. What I don't do is delete it from the array, which swaps a noisy bug for a stale-closure bug."
6 · Guard against the next one "And the exhaustive-deps lint rule stays on."
Close "Dependencies compare by reference, so stabilise the reference at its source or depend on primitives."

Every render: [a, b] inside the list is a new array each time.

react-q10.testing: automatic batching in React 18, and where batching used to stop.
react-q10.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Predict it out loud "B: two in React 17, one in React 18 and later."
2 · Trace the render "In React 17, updates were only batched inside React's own event handlers. Here the two updates happen inside a setTimeout callback, after the click handler has returned, so React 17 processed each one separately: two re-renders."
3 · The rule that decides it "React 18 introduced automatic batching with createRoot. Updates in the same task are batched wherever they happen: timeouts, promises, native event listeners."
4 · Variants that flip it "It flips back to two renders if I wrap one update in flushSync, put them in separate timeouts, or use a legacy root."
5 · The production version "In production, upgrading usually just means fewer renders. The code that breaks is code that read the DOM straight after a setState in a timeout and expected it applied."
Close "Since 18, batching is everywhere, and flushSync is the opt-out."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
function App() {
  const [a, setA] = useState(0);
  const [b, setB] = useState(0);
  const handleClick = () => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      setA(x => x + 1);
      setB(x => x + 1);
    }, 0);
  };
  return <button onClick={handleClick}>{a}{b}</button>;
}

React 17 React 18+

// → re-renders: 1, button shows "11"     (React 19.3, createRoot, jsdom harness)

stages.html:
React 17 React 18+ with createRoot

  • 17: batching tied to React's event system. 18+: batching tied to the scheduler, for any update within the same task, when using createRoot. Legacy ReactDOM.render keeps old behaviour.

When layout must be read synchronously after a state change.

Rare, and it costs performance.

followUps.question: Does batching change the final state?

Changes with batching?

  • StrictMode's double effects in development (Q12).

dontSay: "Batching is only for event handlers" (true only before 18).

react-q11.testing: timing relative to paint, the flicker case, and the cost.
react-q11.trap: "useLayoutEffect is the synchronous, more correct one — use it for safety."
react-q11.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "The difference is timing relative to paint. useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after React commits DOM changes and before the browser paints. useEffect runs after paint."
2 · Where useEffect wins "useEffect is the default for everything that isn't layout: data fetching, subscriptions, timers, logging, analytics. None of that needs to block the frame."
3 · Where useLayoutEffect wins "useLayoutEffect is for one job: measure the DOM and correct it before the user sees the frame. The classic case is a tooltip. I render it, measure its size and the anchor's position, and if it would overflow the viewport I flip it above. In useEffect that shows the wrong position for one frame, a visible flicker."
4 · The deciding question "So the question is: would the user see a wrong frame?"
5 · What I'd pick "My pick is useEffect by default and a layout effect by exception, kept tiny, because it blocks painting, and it doesn't run on the server."
Close "After paint by default; before paint only to measure and correct."

stages.name: Frame the axis
Where useEffect wins
stages.html:
Work Needs to block the frame? Hook
fetching, subscriptions, timers no useEffect
analytics, logging, storage sync no useEffect
measure, then reposition yes useLayoutEffect
  • Fetching, subscriptions, timers, analytics, syncing to storage: doesn't need to block the frame.

stages.name: Where useLayoutEffect wins
stages.html:
Prove it — the tooltip pattern:

function Tooltip({ anchorRect, children }) {
  const ref = useRef(null)
  const [top, setTop] = useState(anchorRect.bottom)
  useLayoutEffect(() => {
    const h = ref.current.getBoundingClientRect().height
    if (anchorRect.bottom + h > window.innerHeight) setTop(anchorRect.top - h)   // flip above
  }, [anchorRect])
  return <div ref={ref} style={{ position: 'fixed', top }}>{children}</div>
}
// with useEffect: one painted frame at the wrong position (flicker); with useLayoutEffect: none

The re-render triggered inside useLayoutEffect is committed before paint, so the user only sees the corrected position.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: would the user see a wrong frame
stages.html:
If it ran after paint, the user would see… Use
a wrong position or size for one frame useLayoutEffect, kept tiny
nothing wrong useEffect
  • Yes → layout effect (keep it tiny). No → useEffect.

stages.html:
Case Hook

everything else effect

  • Popovers, measuring text to truncate, scroll restoration: layout. Everything else: effect. SSR components: guard layout work or use useEffect with a hidden-until-measured style.

followUps.html:

followUps.html:
Layout effects don't run on the server.

  • Render measurement-dependent UI on the client, or use useEffect with the element hidden until measured.

followUps.html:
Before layout effects, for libraries that inject styles.

useInsertionEffectuseLayoutEffectpaintuseEffect

Application code rarely needs it.

followUps.question: INP got worse after a refactor. You find a layout effect doing heavy work. What now?
followUps.html:
Keep only the measurement in the layout effect.

  • Cache measurements that don't change.
  • Verify in the Performance panel that the long task is gone.

react-q12.testing: StrictMode's mount–unmount–mount simulation and why cleanup must be correct.

2 · Trace the render "In development, StrictMode mounts the component and runs its effects, then simulates an unmount, running the cleanups, and mounts again, running the effects a second time. It only happens in development."
3 · The rule that decides it "It is checking that effects are resumable: mounting twice with a cleanup in between must behave like mounting once. React may really unmount and remount components while keeping their state, for example with fast refresh or UI kept alive offscreen."
4 · Variants that flip it "An effect with no cleanup shows the problem at once: a subscription opened twice, a request sent twice."
5 · The production version "In production that same missing cleanup is a leak or duplicate messages: a socket never closed, a listener never removed, a timer never cleared."

react-q13.testing: out-of-order responses, and using effect cleanup to invalidate a request.
react-q13.trap: debouncing as the fix — it reduces the chance, not the bug.
react-q13.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Read the symptom "The results on screen are for a query that is no longer in the box. That is a race."
2 · Measure before guessing "I'd reproduce it by throttling the network, or adding delay so the older request is the slower one."
3 · Rank the suspects "The first suspect is missing invalidation. Two requests are in flight, responses can arrive in any order, and the code sets state with whichever arrives last."
4 · Confirm "A minimal test confirms it: with the first request slower, the stale result wins unless the effect guards against it."
5 · Fix "The fix is for each effect run to invalidate its own request when it is superseded. The cleanup, which runs before the next effect when the query changes, sets an ignore flag, or better, aborts the fetch with an AbortController, which also cancels the network request. Debouncing reduces load but doesn't fix correctness. At scale I'd use a query library that keys requests by the query value."
6 · Guard against the next one "And I'd keep a test where the first response is slow."
Close "Whichever request the user asked for last must win, not whichever responds last."

Suspect Tell

function Results({ query, guard }) {
  const [data, setData] = useState('')
  useEffect(() => {
    let ignore = false
    delay(query === 'a' ? 60 : 10, 'results for ' + query).then(d => { if (!guard || !ignore) setData(d) })
    return () => { ignore = true }
  }, [query])
  return <p>{data}</p>
}
// render query="a", then "ab"; wait 100 ms
// → guard=false  "results for a"    (stale wins)
// → guard=true   "results for ab"   (React 19.3, jsdom harness)

stages.claim: invalidate in cleanup, or let a library key it

useEffect(() => {
  const ctrl = new AbortController()
  fetch(`/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`, { signal: ctrl.signal })
    .then(r => r.json()).then(setResults)
    .catch(e => { if (e.name !== 'AbortError') setError(e) })
  return () => ctrl.abort()
}, [query])
  • Or useQuery({ queryKey: ['search', query], queryFn }).

followUps.question: With the ignore flag but no abort, how many network requests complete when typing 'a','b','c' quickly?

All three complete on the network; only the last result is applied.

ignore flag 3 the last

followUps.html:
Debouncing reduces requests; any two that still overlap can arrive out of order.

React runs the previous effect's cleanup before the next effect.

query changescleanup of the old effect (mark stale, abort)new effect starts its request

It improves how the wait feels; it doesn't order the responses.

abort or ignore the network race

Give each run an ID and only accept tokens for the active one.

react-q14.testing: the argument is evaluated by JavaScript every render; lazy initialisers fix it.
react-q14.trap: answering 1 because "useState only uses the initial value once".
react-q14.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Predict it out loud "B: five times."
2 · Trace the render "useState of buildGrid called is ordinary JavaScript. The argument is evaluated before useState is even called, on every render. React uses the value only on the first render and ignores it afterwards, but the work has already been done."
3 · The rule that decides it "The rule is that function arguments are evaluated eagerly. React can discard the value; it can't prevent the call."
4 · Variants that flip it "The fix is lazy initialisation: pass the function itself, useState of buildGrid without calling it, or an arrow that calls it with arguments. React calls it once, on mount, and never again."
5 · The production version "In production this is an input component that parses local storage, or builds a large structure, on every keystroke. I look for any useState whose argument is a call that reads, parses or builds."
Close "React uses the initial value once, but JavaScript evaluates the argument every render, so pass a function."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
function App() {
  const [grid, setGrid] = useState(buildGrid());
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setN(n + 1)}>{n}</button>;
}

stages.name: Trace the render
stages.html:
Prove it:

// mount + 4 clicks = 5 renders
// → buildGrid called 5 times              (React 19.3, jsdom harness, no StrictMode)
// with useState(buildGrid)
// → 1

  • JavaScript evaluates f(g()) by calling g first. React can only discard the value, not prevent the call.

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.html:
Variant Calls over 5 renders
useState(buildGrid) 1
useState(() => buildGrid(10)) 1
StrictMode dev, lazy initialiser 2 on mount (double render), then none
useMemo(() => buildGrid(), []) 1 (but memo is a cache hint, not a guarantee)

stages.name: The production version
stages.html:
Code Cost per render
useState(JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('draft'))) a storage read and a parse
useState(buildGrid(100)) builds the grid, then throws it away
useState(() => …) nothing after mount
  • useState(JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('draft'))) in an input component parses storage on every keystroke; lazy initialisers fix it.

followUps.question: useState(() => buildGrid()) in StrictMode development — how many calls on mount?
followUps.html:
Two: StrictMode double-invokes render and initialisers in development.

Build Calls on mount
development, StrictMode 2
production 1

followUps.question: "React only runs the initial value once."
followUps.html:
React only uses it once; JavaScript evaluates it every render.

Who Does what, per render
JavaScript evaluates the argument
React keeps the first value, ignores the rest

followUps.question: Why not useMemo for this?
followUps.html:
useMemo is a cache hint; lazy state is guaranteed and updatable.

useMemo(() => build(), []) useState(() => build())
Runs once, guaranteed no: React may discard the cache yes
Can be updated no yes, with the setter

followUps.question: Does useReducer have the same issue?
followUps.html:
Yes, and its third argument is the lazy form.

useReducer(reducer, arg, init)      ← init(arg) runs once, on mount

followUps.question: Where would you spot this in a code review?
followUps.html:
Any useState(someCall(...)) where the call reads, parses or builds.

  • Suggest the lazy form in review.
  • The Profiler shows it as repeated work in every render of that component.

react-q15.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Predict it out loud "B: child effect, then parent effect."
2 · Trace the commit "Rendering goes top-down: the parent renders first and produces the child. But effects run after the commit, bottom-up: a child's effects before its parent's."
3 · The rule that decides it "That is deliberate. When a parent's effect runs, it can rely on all its descendants' DOM nodes, refs and effects already being set up, for example to measure or focus a child element."
4 · Variants that flip it "The order changes across effect types: every layout effect in the tree runs during commit, before paint, and passive effects run after. So a parent's layout effect runs before a child's passive effect."
5 · The production version "In production this is what lets a dialog's effect focus its first input. What I avoid is a child effect that depends on the parent's effect having run first: I pass data down instead."
Close "Render goes down the tree, effects come back up."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
function Parent() {
  useEffect(() => console.log('parent effect'), []);
  return <Child />;
}
function Child() {
  useEffect(() => console.log('child effect'), []);
  return null;
}
  • A: parent effect, child effect · B: child effect, parent effect · C: order is not guaranteed · D: only parent effect

stages.name: Trace the commit
stages.html:
Prove it:

// → child effect, parent effect     (React 19.3, jsdom harness)
Phase Order
render Parent → Child
commit DOM Child's DOM inside Parent's
effects (layout and passive) Child → Parent
cleanups on unmount Parent → Child

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.claim: the parent sees a finished subtree
stages.html:
Order of work:render Parentrender Childcommit DOMChild's effectsParent's effects

React completes work bottom-up, and effects fire in completion order.

  • React completes work bottom-up; effects fire in completion order, so children are ready before parents.

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.html:
Variant Order
both useLayoutEffect child, parent
parent useLayoutEffect, child useEffect parent (layout, before paint), then child (passive)
siblings in tree order, each subtree bottom-up

stages.name: The production version
stages.html:
Pattern Verdict
a parent effect that focuses or measures a child's DOM node safe: the child is set up first
a child effect that needs the parent's effect to have run fragile: it runs before the parent's; pass data as props
parent and child each fetching in an effect a waterfall: hoist or parallelise
  • A dialog's effect can focus its first input because the input's DOM exists; a child effect that depends on the parent's effect having run first is fragile — pass data down instead.

followUps.question: Parent uses useLayoutEffect, child uses useEffect. Order?
followUps.html:
parent layout first, then child effect.

Effect kind Runs
layout effects, whole tree during commit, before paint
passive effects, whole tree after paint

followUps.question: "Parent effects run first because the parent renders first."
followUps.html:
Rendering and effects have different orders.

Phase Order
render parent, then child
effects child, then parent

followUps.question: Why would React design it that way?
followUps.html:
So a parent can safely use its children's DOM and refs in its effect.

  • They are guaranteed to exist by the time the parent's effect runs.

followUps.question: What order do cleanups run on unmount?
followUps.html:
Parent before child: the reverse of setup.

Order
setup child, then parent
cleanup on unmount parent, then child

followUps.question: A child fetches data in an effect and the parent also fetches. What's the problem?
followUps.html:
A request waterfall.

parent mountsparent fetchparent renders the childonly then the child's fetch starts

Hoist fetching to route loaders, or start the requests in parallel (Server Components, query prefetching).

dontSay: Relying on a child effect running after the parent's.

react-q16.testing: refs as a mutable box React doesn't watch, and choosing ref vs state.
react-q16.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "A ref is a plain mutable object with a current property that React keeps stable for the component's lifetime, and React doesn't watch it."
2 · What React does "There is no setter and no scheduling, so changing ref dot current never triggers a render. State goes through setState, which schedules one."
3 · Prove it "A test shows it: three writes to the ref, and the component has still rendered once and still shows zero."
4 · Where it bites "That is a bug the moment the value belongs on screen: the UI shows whatever was current at the last render and silently goes stale. And I don't read or write refs during render, because that makes render impure; I do it in effects and handlers."
5 · What changed by version "In React 19, ref is an ordinary prop on function components, so forwardRef is no longer needed."
Close "Refs are for what the screen doesn't display: a DOM node, a timer ID, an AbortController, the latest callback."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: a mutable box React doesn't watch
stages.html:
"State is watched and triggers renders; a ref is stable storage that doesn't."

Belongs in a ref Belongs in state
a DOM node handle anything shown on screen
a timer or interval ID anything the output is computed from
an AbortController
the latest callback for a subscription

stages.name: What React does
stages.html:
useState useRef
change triggers render yes no
value per render snapshot always latest
use for displayed data handles, IDs, latest values for callbacks

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
function RefBox() {
  renders++
  const ref = useRef(0)
  bump = () => { ref.current++ }
  return <p>{ref.current}</p>
}
// call bump() three times
// → renders: 1, shown: "0"          (React 19.3, jsdom harness)

stages.name: Where it bites
stages.html:
Mistake Symptom
a displayed value kept in a ref the screen is stale until something else re-renders
reading ref.current during render output depends on something React can't track
writing a ref during render breaks under concurrent and StrictMode double renders
  • Displayed values in refs go stale; reading ref.current in render; mutating refs during render (breaks concurrent rendering assumptions).

stages.name: What changed by version
stages.html:
Version Refs
18 and earlier function components need forwardRef to receive a ref
19 ref is a regular prop; a ref callback may return a cleanup function
  • 19: ref is a regular prop for function components (no forwardRef needed); ref callbacks can return a cleanup function.

followUps.question: After bump() ×3, the parent re-renders for another reason. What's shown?
followUps.html:
"3": the next render reads the latest ref.current.

three writesno renderparent re-renders for another reasonthe screen jumps from 0 to 3

The value was never lost, only not displayed: the classic stale-UI bug.

followUps.question: "Use refs to avoid re-renders for performance."
followUps.html:
Only for values that aren't shown.

Value In a ref
not displayed saves pointless renders
displayed trades a render for a wrong UI

followUps.question: How do you keep the latest callback for a subscription?
followUps.html:
Keep it in a ref that is updated in an effect, or use useEffectEvent.

rendereffect stores the newest callback in ref.currentthe long-lived subscription calls ref.current()

followUps.question: How do you track a previous prop value?
followUps.html:
A ref updated in an effect, or state compared during render when it affects output.

Need Pattern
for logging or an effect ref, updated in an effect
changes what is rendered keep the previous value in state and compare in render

followUps.question: In a streaming chat, where do refs help?
followUps.html:
For everything that shouldn't re-render on each token.

  • The AbortController of the active stream.
  • A token buffer flushed to state once per animation frame.
  • The scroll container, for auto-scroll.

dontSay: Reading refs in render for display.

react-q17.testing: shallow prop comparison and reference identity of inline objects and functions.
react-q17.trap: "memo is broken" or "memo does a deep compare".
react-q17.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Predict it out loud "It re-renders every time, because the memo never gets equal props."
2 · Trace the render "React.memo skips a re-render only if every prop is equal by Object.is to last time, a shallow compare. The parent passes a style object literal and an inline arrow function, both created fresh during each render. They look identical, but they are new references."
3 · The rule that decides it "The rule: objects, arrays and functions compare by reference, so the comparison fails every time and the memo is pure overhead."
4 · Variants that flip it "To make memo work, the props must be stable: hoist the constant style object outside the component, and wrap the handler in useCallback. With the React Compiler enabled, these inline values are memoised automatically."
5 · The production version "In production the Profiler shows it: a memoised component rendering, with props changed, style and onSelect. I fix the source of those props, or ask whether the memo is needed at all."
Close "memo compares shallowly, so it only works when the props keep their identity."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
const Child = React.memo(({ style, onSelect }) => {
  console.log('child render');
  return <div style={style} onClick={onSelect} />;
});
function Parent() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={() => setN(n + 1)}>{n}</button>
      <Child style={{ color: 'red' }} onSelect={() => console.log('pick')} />
    </>
  );
}

stages.name: Trace the render
stages.html:
Prove it:

// mount + 2 clicks = 3 parent renders
// → child renders: 3                    (React 19.3, jsdom harness)
Prop Render 1 Render 2 Object.is
style {color:'red'} #1 {color:'red'} #2 false
onSelect fn #1 fn #2 false

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.html:
Prop type Object.is between two renders
number, string, boolean equal if the value is equal
object or array literal never equal: a new reference each render
inline function never equal
JSX passed as children never equal: a new element object
  • memo compares each prop with Object.is; objects, arrays and functions compare by reference.

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.html:
Change Child renders over 3 parent renders
const RED = { color: 'red' } outside + useCallback handler 1
only style hoisted, handler still inline 3
React Compiler enabled 1 (auto-memoized)
children prop as JSX 3 (JSX elements are new objects)

stages.name: The production version
stages.html:
In the Profiler:memoised component still renders"props changed: style, onSelect"fix where those props are created, or remove the memo
  • Profiler shows memoized components rendering with "props changed: style, onSelect". Fix the sources or drop the memo.

followUps.question: You hoist style but pass onSelect={handleSelect} where handleSelect is a plain function inside Parent. Renders?
followUps.html:
Still every time: handleSelect is recreated on each render.

Handler Stable?
a plain function inside Parent no
useCallback with correct dependencies yes
a function defined outside the component yes, if it needs no props or state

followUps.question: "memo deep-compares props."
followUps.html:
It is shallow.

  • A custom comparator can be passed as the second argument.
  • Deep comparison is costly and error-prone, so it is rarely the right fix.

followUps.question: Why does passing children break memo?
followUps.html:
Because JSX creates a new element object on every parent render.

<Child><Icon /></Child>children = a new objectthe prop changed by referencememo fails

followUps.question: Is the failed memo harmful?
followUps.html:
Slightly: a comparison, then the render anyway.

Cost Benefit
a shallow compare per render, plus code noise none

followUps.question: How would you fix a slow list whose rows are memoized but still re-render?
followUps.html:
Find which props change, then stabilise them at the source.

  • Profile to see the changed props.
  • Pass IDs and primitives instead of objects; useCallback for handlers; or adopt the React Compiler.
  • If there are many rows, virtualise first (Q31).

react-q18.testing: memoization as a measured tool, and cheaper structural fixes first.
react-q18.trap: "memo everything to be safe" or "memo is always bad".
react-q18.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "I'd ask for the profile that motivated it. Memoisation is a cache: it trades a comparison on every render and some complexity for skipped render work."
2 · Where memoization wins "It pays off when a component is expensive to render and its props really are stable."
3 · Where it costs "Everywhere else it costs: memory, a comparison each time, dependency arrays that must stay correct, and noise that hides the logic. And blanket useCallback often doesn't even work, because one inline object further up breaks the chain."
4 · The deciding question "So the question is whether the profiler showed this component as a cost. Before memo I'd try structural fixes: move state down, closer to where it is used, and pass expensive subtrees as children so they aren't re-created when a stateful parent changes."
5 · What I'd say in review "In review I'd say: remove it where the profiler shows nothing, keep it on the proven hot spots, and with the React Compiler on React 19 most of it becomes redundant anyway."
Close "Measure, restructure, then memoise what is still hot."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
"Memoization trades comparison cost and maintenance for skipped render work; it's worth it only where that work is big and props are stable."

Memoisation buys Memoisation costs
a skipped render, when props are equal a comparison on every render
a stable reference for a child or an effect memory for the cached value
dependency arrays that can go stale
wrappers that hide intent

stages.name: Where memoization wins
stages.html:
Worth memoising Why
a large list or chart whose inputs rarely change the skipped work is big
a value passed to a memoised child, or used as an effect dependency identity matters there
  • Large lists or charts whose inputs rarely change; values passed to memoized children or used as effect dependencies.

stages.name: Where it costs
stages.html:
Cost Detail
comparison per render props or deps checked every time
stale-deps bugs wrong dependency arrays → stale values
broken chains one unstable prop defeats the whole memo
readability intent buried under wrappers

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
Prove it — the cheaper structural fix (children pattern):

function Page() {
  return <ScrollTracker><ExpensiveTree /></ScrollTracker>   // ExpensiveTree created by Page
}
function ScrollTracker({ children }) {
  const [y, setY] = useState(0)                            // updates often
  useEffect(() => { const f = () => setY(scrollY); addEventListener('scroll', f); return () => removeEventListener('scroll', f) }, [])
  return <div data-y={y}>{children}</div>                  // children element is the same object → not re-rendered
}

ScrollTracker re-renders on every scroll; ExpensiveTree doesn't, with no memo at all, because its element was created by Page, which didn't re-render.

stages.name: What I'd say in review
stages.html:
The order I'd ask for:profilemove state downchildren pattern, split contextsmemo on the proven hot spotsadopt the compiler
  • "Please remove memo/useCallback where the profiler shows no cost; keep it on X and Y where it measurably helps; consider moving state down here; with the compiler we'll drop most of these."

followUps.question: A memoized component receives items={data.filter(x => x.active)} from its parent. Does memo help?
followUps.html:
No: filter returns a new array on every render.

Fix Where
useMemo around the filtered array in the parent
pass data, filter inside the child in the child

followUps.question: "Memoization is free, so wrap everything."
followUps.html:
It costs comparisons, memory and correctness risk.

  • Unmeasured, it often buys nothing.
  • A wrong dependency array turns it into a stale-value bug.

followUps.question: What does the React Compiler change?
followUps.html:
It memoises automatically wherever it can prove the code is pure.

Before With the compiler
memo, useCallback, useMemo by hand everywhere it matters mostly unnecessary (Q40)
what reviews focus on dependency arrays purity

followUps.question: Why does moving state down help?
followUps.html:
Only the component that owns the state, and its subtree, re-render.

state at the page level ─▶ the whole page re-renders
state inside the input component ─▶ only that component re-renders

followUps.question: How do you make this a team standard?
followUps.html:
A short guideline and tooling, not a rule to memo or not.

  • Guideline: profile first; prefer structure; memo only proven hot spots.
  • PR template: a performance check for list and form changes.
  • Compiler and its lint rules, instead of manual memo rules.

dontSay: A review comment without asking for a profile.

react-q19.trap: inventing a difference ("useCallback prevents re-creating the function").
react-q19.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Predict it out loud "Nothing. useCallback of a function and dependencies is exactly useMemo of an arrow returning that function, with the same dependencies."
2 · Trace the equivalence "Both return the same value across renders until a dependency changes. A test shows the two references staying stable together."
3 · The rule that decides it "The rule: both cache one value by dependencies. useMemo caches the result of calling a function; useCallback caches the function itself. It is just the convenient spelling when the value I want to keep stable is a function."
4 · Variants that flip it "Both break the same way: miss a dependency and you get a stale function or value."
5 · The production version "One misconception to correct: useCallback doesn't stop the function being created. The inline function is still created every render; useCallback hands back the previous one. So I use it only where identity matters: a memoised child, an effect dependency, a custom hook that depends on it."
Close "Same mechanism; useCallback is for a stable function reference, useMemo for skipping a computation."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
"useCallback(fn, deps) ≡ useMemo(() => fn, deps)."

useCallback(fn, deps)   ≡   useMemo(() => fn, deps)

stages.name: Trace the equivalence
stages.html:
Prove it:

function Same({ n }) {
  const a = useCallback(() => n, [n])
  const b = useMemo(() => () => n, [n])
  pair.push([a, b])
  return null
}
// render twice with n = 1; compare render 1 vs render 2
// → stable across renders: true true        (React 19.3, jsdom harness)

returns purpose

useCallback(fn, deps) fn itself stable function reference

stages.html:
Variant Result
a dependency is missing both return a stale function or value
React Compiler enabled both mostly unnecessary
dependencies change every render both recompute every time: no benefit
  • Missing a dependency → both return a stale function/value.
  • React Compiler enabled → both mostly unnecessary.

stages.name: The production version
stages.html:
The function goes to useCallback useful?
a memoised child yes
an effect's dependency array yes
a custom hook that depends on identity yes
a DOM element or a non-memoised child no: nothing compares it
  • Callbacks passed to memoized children, used in effect deps, or passed to custom hooks that depend on identity.

followUps.question: const onSave = useCallback(() => save(form), []). What does it save after the user edits the form?
followUps.html:
The original form from the first render: the empty list froze a stale closure.

Dependencies save receives
[] the form as it was at mount
[form] the current form

followUps.question: "useCallback prevents creating a new function each render."
followUps.html:
The function literal is still created; useCallback returns the cached one.

rendernew arrow function createduseCallback compares depsreturns the previous function, discards the new one

followUps.question: When is useCallback pointless?
followUps.html:
When nothing compares the function's identity.

  • A non-memoised child: it re-renders anyway.

followUps.question: Is useMemo a guarantee?

No: it is a performance hint, and React may discard cached values.

Use useMemo for Don't use it for
skipping expensive work; a stable reference correctness: something that must run exactly once

followUps.question: How does the compiler change your reviews here?
followUps.html:
With the compiler, manual memoisation rarely matters.

  • And at dependency arrays wherever manual memo remains.

react-q20.testing: single source of truth, subscribing to history, push vs replace, serialisation.
react-q20.trap: keeping a useState copy synced to the URL with effects.
react-q20.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "First, which state: only what should be shareable, bookmarkable and meaningful to the back button. Filters, tabs, pagination, search."
2 · Constraints "The constraints are that back and forward must work, server rendering must match, typing mustn't flood history, and a hand-edited URL mustn't crash the page."
3 · Baseline design "The API mirrors useState: a value and a setter, with parse, serialise, a default and a history mode. The key decision is that the URL is the single source of truth. The hook keeps no state of its own; it reads the location and subscribes to changes with useSyncExternalStore, listening to popstate and my own navigation event."
4 · Deep-dive "The hard parts are serialisation of typed values with safe parsing, push against replace as an explicit option, batching several params into one navigation, and debouncing text inputs."
5 · Failure modes "The failure to avoid is a useState copy synced to the URL with effects: two sources of truth that drift."
6 · Evolve "In Next.js I'd build on useSearchParams and router replace, since the router owns the URL."
Close "The URL is the state; the hook only reads it and writes it."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: which state belongs in the URL
stages.html:
Put in the URL Keep out of it
filters, search text, sort hover, focus, open menus
current tab, page number unsaved drafts with private data
selected record or conversation ID anything that changes many times a second
  • Shareable, bookmarkable, back-button-meaningful state: filters, tabs, pagination, search. Not ephemeral UI (hover, open menus).

stages.name: Constraints
stages.claim: back and forward, SSR, no spam
stages.html:
Constraint Consequence for the design
back and forward must work subscribe to popstate
server and client must agree a server snapshot; the same parser on both sides
typing must not flood history replace for typing, or debounce and push once
a hand-edited URL must not crash validated parsing with a fallback
  • Back/forward must work; SSR must match; typing shouldn't flood history; invalid URLs must not crash.

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
Prove it — the core, framework-agnostic:

function subscribe(cb) { addEventListener('popstate', cb); addEventListener('urlchange', cb); return () => { removeEventListener('popstate', cb); removeEventListener('urlchange', cb) } }
function useQueryParam(key, { parse = String, serialize = String, fallback, history: mode = 'replace' } = {}) {
  const raw = useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, () => new URLSearchParams(location.search).get(key), () => null)
  const value = raw == null ? fallback : parse(raw)
  const setValue = useCallback(next => {
    const p = new URLSearchParams(location.search); p.set(key, serialize(next))
    window.history[mode === 'push' ? 'pushState' : 'replaceState'](null, '', `?${p}`)
    dispatchEvent(new Event('urlchange'))
  }, [key, serialize, mode])
  return [value, setValue]
}

  • Read from the URL directly, and there is nothing to sync.

Wherever a link should reopen the same view.

links.label: H7 Custom Hooks and the Rules of Hooks

react-q21.testing: tearing under concurrent rendering and the correct subscription primitive.
react-q21.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "It is the correct way to read from a store that lives outside React, such as a Redux or Zustand store, online status, a media query or the URL, and re-render when it changes."
2 · What React does "The problem it solves is tearing. With concurrent rendering React can pause a render halfway through a tree. If the external store changes during that pause, components rendered before it show the old value and components after show the new one. The hook takes a subscribe function and a getSnapshot function. React checks the snapshot during render and, if it changed mid-render, re-renders synchronously so the whole tree is consistent."
3 · Prove it "A small store shows the normal case: two components, one update, both show the same value."
4 · Where it bites "It bites when getSnapshot returns a new object on every call, which loops, or when subscribe isn't a stable function."
5 · What changed by version "It arrived in React 18 with concurrent rendering, and the state libraries use it underneath."
Close "useState plus a subscription in an effect can miss updates and tear; this hook is the supported way."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html: "It lets React read an external store consistently across a whole render, even when rendering is interruptible."

stages.name: What React does
stages.html:
Step Role
subscribe(cb) React registers to be told about changes
getSnapshot() read the current value; must return the same reference if unchanged
during/after render React compares snapshots; if changed mid-render, re-renders synchronously
getServerSnapshot() value used on the server and during hydration

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
const store = { v: 0, subs: new Set(), set(n) { this.v = n; this.subs.forEach(f => f()) },
  subscribe(f) { store.subs.add(f); return () => store.subs.delete(f) }, get: () => store.v }
function A() { const v = useSyncExternalStore(store.subscribe, store.get); return <span>{v}</span> }
// render <A /><A />, then store.set(7)
// → "77", subscribers: 2            (React 19.3, jsdom harness)

Tearing itself needs a concurrent render interrupted mid-tree; it's hard to show in a few lines, which is why the guarantee matters.

stages.name: Where it bites
stages.html:
Mistake Symptom Fix
getSnapshot returns a new object each call an infinite re-render loop, with a "should be cached" warning return a primitive or a cached reference
subscribe defined inline resubscribes on every render define it outside the component, or memoise it
no server snapshot an error or mismatch during server rendering pass getServerSnapshot
  • getSnapshot returning a new object each call → infinite re-render loop ("The result of getSnapshot should be cached").
  • Unstable subscribe function → resubscribes every render; define it outside the component or memoize.

stages.name: What changed by version
stages.html:
Version Status
16, 17 available through a shim
18+ built in; Redux and Zustand use it
  • 18: introduced with concurrent rendering (a shim exists for 16/17). State libraries (Redux, Zustand) adopted it.

followUps.question: getSnapshot = () => ({ online: navigator.onLine }). What happens?

React sees a new object on every call, assumes the store changed, and re-renders repeatedly.

getSnapshot returns Result

navigator.onLine stable: re-renders only on change

followUps.html:
It can miss a change between render and effect, and it can tear.

render reads the storestore changeseffect subscribes (too late: that change is missed)

followUps.question: What is tearing?
followUps.html:
Different parts of the UI showing different versions of the same data in one frame.

  • Cause: the source changed during an interrupted render.
  • Only possible for data React doesn't own.

followUps.question: Should app code use it directly?
followUps.html:
For browser APIs and small custom stores, yes; for application state, use a library built on it.

Source Use
online status, media queries, the URL the hook directly
application state Zustand, Redux

followUps.question: A real-time dashboard pushes prices via WebSocket into a store. How do you connect it to React?
followUps.html:
Keep the socket outside React and let components select what they need.

Hundreds of messages a second must not mean hundreds of renders.

react-q22.testing: two independent reasons — parent re-render and context value identity — and which fix addresses which.
react-q22.trap: "memoize the context value" as the whole fix.
react-q22.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Predict it out loud "There are two reasons, and they need different fixes."
2 · Trace the render "The first: ExpensiveTree is rendered by App, and changing the theme re-renders App. By default React re-renders all children of a component that re-renders, whether or not their props changed. The second: the provider's value is an object literal, new on every App render. Consumers re-render when the value changes identity, so even a memoised tree would still re-render."
3 · The rule that decides it "So the two rules are: a parent's render cascades to its children, and context compares its value by reference."
4 · Variants that flip it "The fix needs both. Memoise the value so it only changes when user changes, and stop the parent's re-render reaching the tree: wrap it in memo, or move the theme state into its own component so App doesn't re-render at all."
5 · The production version "In production this is the single app context with an inline object, which re-renders every consumer on any change. I split contexts by concern and by how often they change."
Close "Two causes: the parent re-rendered, and the context value changed identity."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
function App() {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null);
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState('dark');
  return (
    <AuthCtx.Provider value={{ user, setUser }}>
      <button onClick={() => setTheme(t => (t === 'dark' ? 'light' : 'dark'))} />
      <ExpensiveTree />
    </AuthCtx.Provider>
  );
}

stages.html:
Prove it — renders of the tree over mount + one theme change:

Setup Tree renders
as written (inline value, no memo) 2
memo(ExpensiveTree), inline value 2 (context identity changed)
memo(ExpensiveTree) + useMemo value 1
no memo, useMemo value 2 (parent re-render) 
// (React 19.3, jsdom harness; one theme click after mount)

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.claim: renders cascade, context is by reference
stages.html:
Rule Stopped by
a re-rendering component re-renders its children memo with equal props, or elements passed in from above
a context consumer re-renders when value changes by Object.is a stable value; memo does not help
  • A re-rendering component re-renders its children unless they bail out (memo with equal props, or elements passed from above).
  • Context consumers re-render when value changes by Object.is, regardless of memo.

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.html:
Variant Effect

pass ExpensiveTree as children from above not re-created by the provider component
split AuthStateCtx / AuthDispatchCtx setter-only consumers never re-render for user changes

stages.html:

one "AppContext" with an inline object split by concern and by update frequency
