high-frequency data in context a store with selectors (Q23)
  • A single "AppContext" with an inline object re-renders every consumer on any change. Split by concern and update frequency; for high-frequency data, use a store with selectors (Q23).

followUps.question: You memoize the value with useMemo(..., [user]) but don't memo ExpensiveTree. Theme change: does it re-render?
followUps.html:
Yes: its parent re-rendered, and a non-memoised child re-renders with it.

Setup Tree renders on a theme change
useMemo value, no memo yes
useMemo value and memo no

followUps.question: "Memoize the context value and you're done."
followUps.html:
Necessary, not sufficient.

  • It fixes the context-identity cause.
  • It doesn't stop the parent's re-render cascading to children that aren't memoised.

followUps.question: Why split state and dispatch contexts?
followUps.html:
So components that only call the setter don't re-render when the state changes.

Context Value Changes
state user when the user changes
dispatch setUser never

followUps.question: Does context have selectors?
followUps.html:
No: every consumer re-renders when the value changes.

  • For selective subscriptions use a store (Zustand, Redux).
  • Or a library such as use-context-selector.

followUps.question: How would you find this in a real app?
followUps.html:
The Profiler, with "Why did this render?".

It says Fix
"context changed" stabilise or split the value
"parent rendered" memo, or move the state

Then measure the drop in commit time.

dontSay: Only one of the two causes.
"Context re-renders everything" without the identity detail.

links.label: ST2 Context Patterns and the Performance Cliff

react-q23.testing: Context as dependency injection, not a state manager, and its no-selector re-render model.
react-q23.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Context is dependency injection for a subtree. It lets deeply nested components read a value without passing props through every level. It removes prop drilling; it doesn't give fine-grained subscriptions."
2 · Where Context wins "It is great for values that change rarely and are needed widely: theme, locale, the current user, feature flags, and injecting services such as an API client."
3 · Where it's the wrong instinct "It is the wrong instinct for high-frequency or large state. Context has no selectors: when the value changes, every consumer re-renders, even if it uses one field. It is also wrong for server data, which belongs in a query cache, and for avoiding two levels of props, where composition is clearer."
4 · The deciding question "So I ask how often the value changes, and how many components read it."
5 · What I'd pick "I use context for stable, widely needed values, split providers by update frequency, and use a store with selectors when many components need slices of frequently changing state."
Close "Context is for injecting stable values, not for managing fast-changing state."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
"Context removes prop drilling; it doesn't give fine-grained subscriptions."

Props Context Store with selectors
Reaches deep components by passing through each level directly directly
Who re-renders on a change the components that receive the prop every consumer only components whose selected slice changed
Best for nearby data stable, widely read values shared state that changes often

stages.claim: how often, and how many read it
stages.html:
Prove it — every consumer re-renders, even for fields it ignores:

const Ctx = createContext(null)

function Cursor() { const { pos } = useContext(Ctx); renders.cursor++; return pos.x }
// value = { user, pos } updated 60×/s for mouse moves → Name re-renders 60×/s too

server data a query library (Q24)
two or three levels of props props, or children composition

Yes: the whole value changed identity.

Consumer reads Re-renders when user changes

followUps.html:
It replaces prop drilling.

Context Redux or Zustand

test<Ctx.Provider value={fake}>component under test

followUps.html:
Not in context.

links.label: ST2 Context Patterns and the Performance Cliff

react-q24.testing: splitting state by category rather than picking one library.
react-q24.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "I don't pick one library. I split state by category, because each category has different needs."
2 · Server state "Server state is data that lives on the server: users, orders, conversation history. It needs caching, deduplication, background refetching and invalidation after mutations. That is a query library's job: TanStack Query, or Server Components plus the framework cache. Most global state in older Redux apps was really this."
3 · Shared client state "Shared client state is what the server doesn't know about but distant components need: a draft that spans panels, a selection. For a small slice, Zustand, because selectors mean components re-render only for what they read. Redux Toolkit when the organisation standardises on it, or many teams share one large client state."
4 · Local and URL state "Local state stays local in useState or useReducer, and anything that should survive a refresh or be shareable goes in the URL. Context is fine for low-frequency values like theme."
5 · What I'd pick here "For an AI product I'd pick TanStack Query for conversations and runs, Zustand for the composer and streaming UI state, the URL for the selected conversation, and local state for the rest."
Close "Choose by the kind of state, not by the library."

stages.claim: what kind of state is it
stages.html:
Category Examples Tool

shared client state cross-panel drafts, selections Zustand (small) / Redux Toolkit (large, standardised)
local UI state open/closed, input value useState / useReducer
URL state filters, tabs, IDs search params
low-frequency globals theme, locale, auth Context

stages.html:
A server-state tool provides Hand-written in a client store
deduplication of identical requests manual
stale-while-revalidate, refetch on focus manual
invalidation after a mutation manual
retries, pagination manual
  • Dedupe, stale-while-revalidate, invalidation after mutations, retries, pagination — built in.

stages.html:
Prove it — a Zustand slice with selector-based subscriptions:

const useComposer = create(set => ({
  draft: '', streamingRunId: null,
  setDraft: draft => set({ draft }),
  startRun: id => set({ streamingRunId: id }),
}))
function SendButton() { const running = useComposer(s => s.streamingRunId !== null); return <button disabled={running}>Send</button> }
// 3 draft updates → SendButton renders stay at 1; startRun → 2   (React 19.3, zustand 5.0.15, jsdom harness)

Where a piece of state goes:used by one component?local
Otherwise:shareable or should survive a refresh?URLelse lift only as far as needed
  • Colocate by default; lift only as far as needed; URL for shareable state (Q20).

State in an AI chat product Home
conversations, runs, message history TanStack Query

Far more code in Redux.

Redux TanStack Query
Add a user a thunk; pending, fulfilled and rejected reducers useMutation
Refresh the list update the cache by hand, or refetch by hand invalidateQueries(['users']) in onSuccess

followUps.html:
Redux Toolkit is fine for large shared client state.

  • Still good for: strict update patterns, devtools, many teams on one store.
  • What is outdated: using it as a server cache.

followUps.question: Why Zustand over Context for shared state?
followUps.html:
Selectors.

Context Zustand
Re-render on a change every consumer only components whose selected slice changed
Provider nesting yes none
Usable outside React no yes

followUps.html:
It is Redux Toolkit's server-state layer.

App Sensible choice
already on Redux RTK Query
otherwise TanStack Query

followUps.question: How do you defend this to a team used to "everything in Redux"?
followUps.html:
Show it on one feature, then write the rule down.

  • Show the boilerplate and the stale-data bugs in the server-data slices.
  • Migrate one feature to a query library as the reference.
  • A one-page rule of which state goes where (Q28).

links.label: ST4 Server State vs Client State

react-q25.testing: server state as a cache of data you don't own, and the features that implies.
react-q25.trap: "server state is just global state you fetched."
react-q25.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "Server state is data whose source of truth is on the server. I don't own it, other users and processes change it, and my copy is always a snapshot that may be stale. Client state is data the browser owns: a draft, an open panel."
2 · Mechanism "Treating server state as client state, fetch once and put it in Redux, means hand-building everything a cache needs: loading and error states, deduplicating identical requests, deciding when data is stale, refetching, invalidating after mutations, retries. Query libraries are caches keyed by the request. Components declare what they need; the library dedupes, caches, revalidates in the background, and mutations invalidate keys."
3 · Where it breaks "It breaks when the same data sits under two different keys, when the stale time is wrong for the data, or when query data is mirrored into another store."
4 · How I've used it "In use: a stale time per resource, prefetch on hover, and no API data in Redux."
5 · Adjacent concept "In the Next.js App Router, Server Components and the framework cache take over part of this role."
Close "Server state is a cache problem, and freshness is the hard part, not storage."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.claim: a local copy of remote truth
stages.html:
"Server state is a cache of data you don't own; its core problem is freshness, not storage."

Server state Client state
Source of truth the server the browser
Can change without you yes no
Core problem freshness where to keep it
Examples users, orders, history a draft, an open panel, a selection

stages.html:
Feature Hand-rolled in Redux Query library
dedupe identical requests manual automatic by key
stale-while-revalidate manual built in (staleTime)
refetch on focus/reconnect manual built in
invalidate after mutation manual invalidateQueries(key)

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.html:
Prove it — the whole data layer for a list and a mutation:

function Users() {
  const { data, isPending, error } = useQuery({ queryKey: ['users'], queryFn: fetchUsers, staleTime: 30_000 })
  const qc = useQueryClient()
  const add = useMutation({ mutationFn: createUser, onSuccess: () => qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['users'] }) })
  if (isPending) return <Spinner />
  if (error) return <ErrorView error={error} />
  return <List users={data} onAdd={add.mutate} />
}
  • Breaks when keys are inconsistent (the same data under two keys), staleTime is wrong for the data, or you mirror query data into another store.

reference data (countries, plans) long rarely changes
a dashboard list tens of seconds fresh enough, few refetches
a live status zero, or polling must be current

Plus prefetch on hover for likely navigation, and optimistic updates for quick actions (Q26).

  • Dashboards and admin tools: staleTime per resource, prefetch on hover, optimistic updates for quick actions (Q26), and no server data in Redux.

  • In App Router, many reads move to the server (RSC fetch + cache); client query libraries remain for interactive, client-driven data (Q37).

three components, same keyone requestall three subscribe to the same cache entry

followUps.html:
No: that creates a second source of truth that won't refetch or invalidate.

  • Derive from the query, or select from it.

History is server state; the streaming message is client state until it finishes.

Data Kind
conversation history, run status queries, invalidated on completion

react-q26.testing: rollback correctness and out-of-order concurrent mutations.
react-q26.trap: optimistic UI with no failure path.
react-q26.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "An optimistic update shows the expected result immediately, the like count goes up, before the server confirms, and then reconciles with the server's response. It makes the UI feel instant for actions that almost always succeed."
2 · How it works "The shape is: take a snapshot, apply the change locally, send the request, then reconcile on success or roll back on error."
3 · Prove it "With TanStack Query that is onMutate to snapshot and apply, onError to restore, and onSettled to invalidate."
4 · Where it bites "It bites in two ways. First, rollback: on failure I must restore exactly the earlier state and tell the user, and a careless snapshot can wipe out a second change. Second, ordering: like, unlike, like in quick succession puts three requests in flight, and if each response overwrites local state, the UI settles on whichever returned last, not on what the user did last. So I send the intended final state, not a toggle, serialise mutations per entity, and refetch once they settle."
5 · What changed by version "In React 19, useOptimistic handles the display side and reverts automatically when the action finishes."
Close "Optimistic UI is a prediction; the design is what happens when the prediction is wrong or late."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
"Optimistic UI predicts the server's answer; correctness depends on rollback and ordering."

Pessimistic Optimistic
The UI changes after the server responds immediately
Feels laggy on a slow network instant
Needs a spinner a rollback path and ordering rules
Pick when the action often fails, or the server computes the result the action almost always succeeds

stages.name: How it works
Prove it
stages.html:
useMutation({
  mutationFn: toggleLike,
  onMutate: async ({ postId, liked }) => {
    await qc.cancelQueries({ queryKey: ['post', postId] })
    const prev = qc.getQueryData(['post', postId])
    qc.setQueryData(['post', postId], p => ({ ...p, liked, likes: p.likes + (liked ? 1 : -1) }))
    return { prev }
  },
  onError: (_e, { postId }, ctx) => qc.setQueryData(['post', postId], ctx.prev),
  onSettled: (_d, _e, { postId }) => qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['post', postId] }),
})

stages.name: Where it bites
stages.html:
Bite Symptom Guard
rollback UI shows unsaved data, or rollback wipes another change per-mutation snapshots, invalidate on settle, error toast
out-of-order responses final state ≠ user's last action send absolute state (liked: true), serialise per entity, idempotency keys, refetch on settle

stages.name: What changed by version
stages.html:
Version Tool
18 and earlier library callbacks (onMutate, onError, onSettled) or hand-written state
19 useOptimistic(state, updateFn): shows optimistic state during an action or transition, then falls back to the real state
  • React 19: useOptimistic(state, updateFn) shows optimistic state during an action/transition and falls back to real state when it settles.

followUps.question: 🧪 User clicks Like (request A, slow), then Unlike (request B, fast). B succeeds, then A succeeds. With toggle semantics, what's the final server state?
followUps.html:
It depends on the order the server processes them, not the order of the clicks.

Sent as If A is processed after B
toggle the post ends liked, though the user unliked
absolute intent (liked: false), serialised per post the post ends unliked

followUps.question: "Optimistic updates are just setting state early."
followUps.html:
That is the easy half.

  • The design is the failure path and the ordering path.
  • Without them the UI shows data the server rejected.

followUps.question: When shouldn't you be optimistic?
followUps.html:
When failure is likely, costly, or the server decides the result.

Case Show instead
validation often fails a pending state
payments, irreversible actions a pending state and confirmation
server-computed values (prices, IDs) a placeholder

followUps.question: Why cancel in-flight queries in onMutate?
followUps.html:
So an earlier refetch can't land after the optimistic write and overwrite it.

refetch in flightoptimistic writestale refetch arrivesthe UI flips back

Cancelling the refetch removes the third step.

followUps.question: In an AI chat, is sending a message optimistic?
followUps.html:
The user's message, yes; the assistant's reply, no.

Part Behaviour
user message appears at once with a pending marker and a client ID
assistant reply can't be predicted: it streams
on failure keep the message, mark it, offer retry

links.label: ST4 Server State vs Client State

react-q27.testing: explicit transitions, testable pure logic, and a stable dispatch.
react-q27.trap: "useReducer is for big state, useState for small."
react-q27.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Mechanically they are the same thing: useState is implemented with a reducer. What useReducer buys is structure."
2 · Where useState wins "useState stays better for independent, simple values: a toggle, an input, a selected tab."
3 · Where useReducer wins "With a reducer, transitions become explicit. Instead of scattered setter calls that must stay consistent, I dispatch named events, submit started, submit failed, and one pure function decides how every field changes. That makes impossible states harder to create, like loading true with an error still set, and the function is testable without rendering. And dispatch is stable across renders, so it goes into effect dependencies or memoised children without useCallback."
4 · The deciding question "So I ask whether several fields change together, or the next state depends on the current one in a non-trivial way."
5 · What I'd pick "I'd pick a reducer for lifecycles: an async form, a wizard, a chat composer's run. And useState for the rest."
Close "It is about coupled transitions, not about how big the state is."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
"Same engine; useReducer centralises how state changes."

useState useReducer
Update setX(value) at the call site dispatch({ type }); one function decides
Several fields together several setters that must agree one transition
Testable without React no yes: a pure function
Stable function to pass down the setter dispatch
Pick when independent values coupled fields, lifecycles

stages.name: Where useState wins
stages.html:
Value Why useState is enough
a toggle one field, two values
an input's text independent of other state
the selected tab set directly from an event
  • A toggle, an input value, a selected tab.

stages.name: Where useReducer wins
stages.html:
Prove it — a pure, testable transition function:

function submitReducer(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'start':   return { status: 'submitting', error: null }
    case 'success': return { status: 'done', error: null }
    case 'fail':    return { status: 'idle', error: action.error }
    default:        return state
  }
}
console.log(submitReducer({ status: 'submitting', error: 'x' }, { type: 'success' }))
// → { status: 'done', error: null }    (plain JS, no React needed)

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
Sign Choice
two or more fields must change together reducer
some combinations must never exist (loading with error) reducer
each value changes independently useState
  • Yes, or transitions have rules → reducer. No → useState.

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.html:
A run's lifecycle as states:idlestreamingdone
And the other exits:streamingerror, oraborted
  • Reducer for async forms, wizards, streaming run state (idle → streaming → done | error | aborted); useState elsewhere; a store when the state must be shared widely.

followUps.question: Is dispatch a new function on each render?
followUps.html:
No: React guarantees dispatch is stable for the component's lifetime.

Function Stable across renders
dispatch, a useState setter yes
a handler defined in the component no, unless memoised

followUps.question: "useReducer is for complex/large state."
followUps.html:
It is for coupled transitions, not size.

  • A big object of independent fields can be several useStates.
  • Two fields that must agree already justify a reducer.

followUps.question: Can reducers have side effects?
followUps.html:
No: they must be pure.

  • React may call a reducer twice in StrictMode.
  • Side effects go in handlers, or in effects that react to the new state.

followUps.question: useReducer + Context — is that Redux?
followUps.html:
A small version of it.

useReducer + context Redux
Selectors no yes
Middleware, devtools no yes
Fine for low-frequency shared state large shared state

followUps.question: How would you model a streaming AI run?
followUps.html:
A reducer over events, with states that make illegal combinations impossible.

  • Events: start, token, toolCall, done, error, abort.
  • Illegal by construction: tokens after done.
  • Tested by replaying recorded event sequences.

react-q28.testing: classify before refactoring, a written rule, and incremental strangling with guardrails.
react-q28.trap: proposing a rewrite or a new library.
react-q28.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd classify before I refactor. First an inventory: for each piece of state, where is it held, who writes it, and how many copies exist. That usually shows most of the swamp is server data copied into Redux and context."
2 · Constraints "The constraint is that features keep shipping, so the migration has to be incremental, reversible, and enforced automatically."
3 · Baseline plan "Then a one-page rule the team agrees on: server data in the query cache, shared client state in one store, local state local, shareable state in the URL, context only for low-frequency globals. Every piece of state has exactly one owner. And I strangle it one vertical feature at a time, starting with a pilot that becomes the reference implementation."
4 · Deep-dive "New code must follow the rule, enforced by lint: an import restriction that blocks new use of the old slices."
5 · Failure modes "What fails is the big-bang rewrite, and adding a new library as the fix, which becomes one more copy."
6 · Evolve "I'd track legacy usages trending down, and with forty contributors I'd treat the social side as part of the work: an RFC, office hours, a named owner."
Close "Classify, write the rule, migrate by feature, and let lint hold the line."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
State Holders today Category Target owner
current user Redux + AuthContext server + auth query cache (+ auth context for session)
orders list Redux slice + component state server query cache
filters Redux + URL + local URL-worthy URL
editor draft Context + local shared client one store

stages.name: Constraints
stages.html:
Constraint Consequence
features keep shipping incremental migration, no freeze
40 contributors the rule must be enforced by tooling, not by memory
behaviour nobody documented characterisation tests before touching a flow
mistakes will happen each step reversible, behind a flag where behaviour changes
  • Features keep shipping; migration must be incremental and reversible; rules must be enforceable automatically.

stages.name: Baseline plan
Deep-dive
stages.html:
Prove it — an ESLint guard on deprecated state paths:

// .eslintrc — block new imports of legacy slices outside allow-listed files
rules: {
  'no-restricted-imports': ['error', { paths: [
    { name: '@/store/ordersSlice', message: 'Use useOrdersQuery() — see docs/state-rules.md' },
  ] }],
}
  • Plus: codemods for mechanical moves, CODEOWNERS on the state layer, a dashboard counting remaining usages.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Failure Why it happens Guard
big-bang rewrite stalls feature work continues underneath it migrate by vertical feature
a new library becomes a fourth copy it was added, nothing was removed (Q44) every migration deletes the old source
every feature half-migrated migrating layer by layer finish one feature end to end
behaviour regressions no tests on the old behaviour characterisation tests first
  • Big-bang rewrite stalls; a new library added as "the fix" becomes a fourth copy (Q44); migrating by layer leaves every feature half-migrated; no tests → behaviour regressions.

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
Metric Reads
imports of legacy slices, over time progress
duplicated sources of the same data remaining risk
stale-data bugs in migrated features whether it worked
developer feedback on the rule whether it will last
  • Count of duplicated state sources, legacy import usages over time, bug rate in migrated features, and developer feedback on the rule.

followUps.question: After migrating orders to TanStack Query, an old component still reads state.orders from Redux. What happens after a user creates an order?
followUps.html:
That component shows old data: the duplicate-source bug.

create orderquery cache invalidated and refetchedthe Redux copy is untouchedthe old component is stale

Migrate or bridge that component, then delete the slice.

followUps.question: "Rewrite state management from scratch."
followUps.html:
Rewrites stall under continuing feature work.

Rewrite Incremental, with a reference feature
Ships value at the end, if ever at every step
Undocumented behaviour broken covered by tests as you go

followUps.question: Why migrate by vertical feature?
followUps.html:
A fully migrated feature is a working example that can be verified.

  • It removes duplication end to end.
  • Layer by layer leaves everything half done.

followUps.question: How do you get 40 people to follow the rule?
followUps.html:
Make the right way the easiest way.

  • A reference implementation to copy.
  • Templates or generators.
  • Lint errors on the old way.
  • A review checklist.

followUps.question: How long and how do you report progress?
followUps.html:
About a quarter for a large app, reported as risk reduction.

Report Shows
legacy usage count trending down progress
stale-data incidents risk removed
feature velocity the cost of the work

react-q29.testing: profile first, reason about why each component rendered, structural fixes before memo.
react-q29.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Read the symptom "Typing that lags is an interaction-latency problem: each keystroke causes a long task."
2 · Measure before guessing "I start by measuring, with the React DevTools Profiler recording while I type and the why-did-this-render option on. That tells me, per component, whether it rendered because of its own state, its parent, a prop or a context, and how long each commit took."
3 · Rank the suspects "Then I decide whether the problem is breadth, many components rendering, or depth, a few doing expensive work. The usual cause of breadth is state living too high: the input's value is stored in a page-level component or a context, so every keystroke re-renders the page."
4 · Confirm "The structural fix confirms it: move the input state down into the search box, and pass only what the page needs."
5 · Fix "For the results list, which really does depend on the query, I keep the input urgent and render the results at lower priority with useDeferredValue, and virtualise if it is long. Memoisation comes after that, on the components the profiler shows as costly."
6 · Guard against the next one "Then I re-measure commit time per keystroke and INP, and watch INP by route in the field."
Close "Profile, fix where the state lives, lower the priority of heavy dependents, and memoise last."

stages.name: Read the symptom
stages.html:
Sign Means
characters appear late while typing the main thread is busy during the keystroke
poor INP on this route real users feel it
a long task per keystroke in the Performance panel render or commit is too slow
  • Poor INP on the search page; each keystroke causes a long task.

stages.name: Measure before guessing
stages.html:
Tool What it shows
React DevTools Profiler + "why did this render" which components, why, how long
Chrome Performance panel long tasks per keystroke
web-vitals INP (field) real users' interaction latency

stages.name: Rank the suspects
stages.html:
Profiler says Suspect Fix
"parent rendered" ×60 state too high move state down / composition
"context changed" input value in context local state; split context
one component 40 ms expensive render memoize calculation, virtualise
results list slow urgent + heavy together useDeferredValue

stages.name: Confirm
stages.html:
Prove it — state moved down, results deferred:

function SearchPage() {                      // no longer holds keystroke state
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('')
  const deferred = useDeferredValue(query)
  return <><SearchBox onChange={setQuery} /><Results query={deferred} /><Sidebar /><Feed /></>
}
const Results = memo(function Results({ query }) { /* expensive filtering + list */ })
  • Typing updates query urgently; Results re-renders with the deferred value in a lower-priority pass that yields to new keystrokes. Sidebar and Feed still re-render with SearchPage unless the input state moves into SearchBox itself.

stages.name: Fix
stages.html:
Order of fixes:move state down, or compositionuseDeferredValue or a transition for heavy dependentsvirtualise long liststargeted memo with stable propsReact Compiler where adopted
  1. Move state down / composition. 2. useDeferredValue or useTransition for heavy dependents. 3. Virtualise long lists. 4. Targeted memo with stable props. 5. React Compiler where adopted.

stages.name: Guard against the next one
stages.html:
Guard Catches
INP by route in field monitoring regressions real users feel
a test that counts renders for a key interaction state creeping back up the tree
a review rule on where input state lives the cause, before it ships
  • INP in field monitoring by route; a performance test recording render counts for key interactions; review rule on where input state lives.

followUps.question: The input's value lives in a Context read by 60 components. You wrap all 60 in memo. Does it help?
followUps.html:
No: context consumers re-render when the value changes, whatever memo says.

Cause of the render Does memo stop it?
the parent rendered yes, with equal props
the context value changed no

Move the input value out of the context.

followUps.question: "memo everything, then profile."
followUps.html:
Backwards.

Wrong:memo everythingprofilestill slow, now harder to read
Right:profilefix structurememo the few proven hot spots

followUps.question: useDeferredValue vs debounce?
followUps.html:
Debounce waits a fixed time; a deferred value renders as soon as there is time.

Debounce useDeferredValue
Delay fixed, even on a fast device adapts to the device
Stale work still runs after the delay interrupted by newer input
Still useful for network requests rendering

followUps.question: How do you prove the fix to others?
followUps.html:
With before-and-after numbers.

  • Profiler: commit duration and render count per keystroke.
  • Field data: INP at the 75th percentile after release.

followUps.question: Same symptom in a chat input while a response streams. Cause and fix?
followUps.html:
Streaming tokens are updating state high in the tree, so the composer re-renders on every token.

  • Isolate the streaming message in its own leaf, fed by a per-frame buffer.
  • Keep composer state local.
  • Defer the transcript list.

react-q30.testing: state is preserved by type + position; a key creates a new identity.
react-q30.trap: answer A — resetting with an effect.
react-q30.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Predict it out loud "B: give the editor a key equal to the document ID."
2 · Trace the render "React preserves a component's state for as long as the same component type sits at the same position in the tree. Switching the document only changes a prop, so the Editor instance, and its draft state, survives."
3 · The rule that decides it "The rule is that identity is type plus position plus key. Changing a prop never resets state; a new key does."
4 · Variants that flip it "With the key, React treats each document as a different instance: it unmounts the old editor and mounts a fresh one with fresh state. An effect that clears the draft also works, but it renders once with the stale draft and again cleared, and it has to be extended for every new piece of state. Memo has no effect on state at all."
5 · The production version "In production I key record panes, per-item forms and chat composers by the record's ID. If drafts should survive switching, I store them in a map keyed by ID instead."
Close "To reset a component, change its identity with a key."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
function Editor({ docId }) {
  const [draft, setDraft] = useState('');
  return <textarea value={draft} onChange={e => setDraft(e.target.value)} />;
}
// parent
<Editor docId={selectedId} />
  • A: add useEffect(() => setDraft(''), [docId]) · B: render <Editor key={docId} docId={selectedId} /> · C: move draft to the parent · D: wrap Editor in React.memo

stages.name: Trace the render
stages.html:
Prove it:

// type "draft for a" in doc a, then switch to doc b
// → without key: "draft for a"
// → key={docId}: ""                 (React 19.3, jsdom harness)

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.html:
What changed between renders State
a prop kept
the component type at that position reset
the key reset
  • Props changing never resets state; a new key does (Q4).

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.claim: the effect and memo fall short
stages.html:
Option Result
A: effect resets works, but an extra render with the stale draft and fragile as state grows
B: key fresh instance, all state reset
C: lift draft to parent works if the parent stores drafts per doc (e.g. a map) — useful to keep unsaved drafts
D: memo no effect on state

stages.name: The production version
stages.html:
Requirement Pattern
a clean form per selected record key={recordId}
drafts that survive switching drafts[recordId] in the parent or a store
a composer per conversation key={conversationId}, or a draft store keyed by it
  • Record detail panes, chat composers per conversation, forms per selected item: key by the record ID. If drafts must survive switching, store them in a map keyed by ID instead.

followUps.question: With key={docId}, the Editor also has an expensive useMemo. What happens on switch?
followUps.html:
It recomputes: the new instance has no cached value.

With key={docId} On switch
state reset
useMemo cache empty: computed again

Usually fine. If not, cache per document outside the component.

followUps.question: "Use an effect to reset the state when the prop changes."
followUps.html:
It renders the stale state first, then resets it.

Effect that resets Key
Renders on switch two, the first with the old draft one, fresh
New state added later must be added to the effect reset automatically

followUps.question: Does a key remount the DOM too?
followUps.html:
Yes: the old DOM subtree is removed and a new one created.

  • Focus and scroll inside it reset too.

followUps.question: When would you choose option C?
followUps.html:
When users expect unsaved drafts to survive switching.

switch documentthe parent keeps drafts[docId]switch backthe draft is still there

followUps.question: In a chat app, conversation A's half-typed message appears in conversation B. Fix?
followUps.html:
Either a clean slate or a draft per conversation.

Product decision Code
start empty each time <Composer key={conversationId} />
keep a draft per conversation a draft store keyed by conversation ID

react-q31.testing: rendering less beats rendering faster; knowing virtualisation's costs.
react-q31.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "The fastest row is the one you never render. With ten thousand rows the DOM itself is the cost: layout, style recalculation and memory, before React is involved."
2 · Virtualisation "Option one is virtualisation: render only the rows in the viewport plus a small overscan, and recycle them as the user scrolls. Tens of thousands of nodes become a few hundred. The trade-offs: variable row heights need measuring, find-in-page and printing don't see off-screen rows, and accessibility needs row counts and indexes set explicitly."
3 · Server-side paging "Option two is to do less on the client: server-side pagination, filtering and sorting, so the browser never holds ten thousand rows. The trade-off is a request per interaction, so it needs good loading states and a cache."
4 · Cheaper rows "Option three is cheaper rows: memoised rows with stable props, no heavy formatting in render. These are the smallest wins."
5 · What I'd pick "My pick: virtualise the table, push filtering and sorting to the server if the data really is large, and profile before touching row-level memoisation."
Close "Reduce the number of DOM nodes before optimising each one."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
"Reduce the number of DOM nodes before optimising each one."

Option Cuts Costs
virtualisation DOM nodes, by hundreds of times find-in-page, print, variable heights, accessibility work
server-side paging and filtering rows shipped at all a request per interaction
cheaper rows per-row render time little: also the smallest gain

stages.name: Virtualisation
stages.html:
Prove it — the node arithmetic (illustrative):

10,000 rows × 8 cells = 80,000 cells (+ wrappers) in the DOM
Viewport 800 px / 36 px rows ≈ 23 visible + 10 overscan ≈ 33 rows × 8 = 264 cells
→ ~300× fewer nodes to lay out and style
Cost Mitigation
variable heights measure rows (dynamic virtualisers)
Ctrl+F / print provide search in-app; print view
accessibility role="grid", aria-rowcount, keyboard navigation

stages.name: Server-side paging
stages.html:
Flow:user sorts or filtersrequest with cursor and filterserver returns one pageprevious page stays visible while loading
Practice Why
cursor pagination stable under inserts
prefetch the next page paging feels instant
a query cache keyed by filter and page going back is free
  • Cursor pagination, server sort/filter, prefetch the next page, keep previous page visible during loading.

stages.name: Cheaper rows
stages.html:
Lever Effect
memo rows with stable props (IDs, not objects) rows skip re-rendering
precomputed formatted values no date or number formatting in render
content-visibility: auto the browser skips off-screen layout, for lists that aren't virtualised
  • memo rows with stable props (ids, not objects); precompute formatted values; avoid inline heavy components per cell; content-visibility: auto for non-virtualised lists.

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.claim: virtualise, and let the server filter
stages.html:
Dataset Pick
thousands of rows already on the client virtualise
far more than the client should hold server-side sort and filter, plus virtualise what is loaded
after both profile scrolling, then consider row-level memo
  • Virtualised grid + server-side sort/filter for big datasets; profile scroll with the Performance panel (frame rate, long tasks) before and after.

followUps.question: 🧪 After virtualising, a user presses Ctrl+F for a value in row 9,000. What happens?
followUps.html:
The browser can't find it: that row isn't in the DOM.

Feature lost with virtualisation Replacement
Ctrl+F in-app search that scrolls to the match
printing a separate print view

followUps.question: "memo every row and it'll be smooth."
followUps.html:
Memo reduces React re-renders, not the cost of 80,000 DOM nodes.

  • Scrolling a huge DOM is slow with zero re-renders.
  • Virtualise first.

followUps.question: Why is scroll janky even without re-renders?
followUps.html:
The browser's own work on a huge DOM.

  • Layout and painting of tens of thousands of nodes.
  • Scroll handlers that do work.
  • Images loading as they come into view.

followUps.question: Pagination or infinite scroll?
followUps.html:
By how people use the data.

Use Choice
a table people navigate and refer to ("page 3") pagination
a feed infinite scroll

Either way, virtualise a long loaded list.

followUps.question: A log viewer streams 50 new lines per second into a list. Design?
followUps.html:
Virtualise, batch the appends, and cap what is kept.

  • Buffer new lines and flush once per animation frame.
  • A ring buffer caps retained lines; "load older" comes from the server.
  • Auto-scroll only when the user is already at the bottom.

dontSay: Shipping 10,000 rows when the server can filter.

links.label: D4 Large Lists and Noisy Input

react-q32.testing: splitting where it pays, and hiding the latency you introduced.
react-q32.trap: splitting everything into tiny chunks that load in a waterfall with spinners.
react-q32.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I start from what the first screen needs. Everything required for its first paint stays in the main chunk; everything else is a candidate."
2 · Constraints "The constraint is that splitting doesn't remove latency, it moves it to the moment the user asks for the feature."
3 · Baseline boundaries "So I split at three kinds of boundary: routes, which frameworks do automatically; surfaces behind a click, such as modals, editors and settings panels; and heavy libraries used in one place, such as a rich-text editor or a charting library. And I hide the latency: prefetch the chunk on hover or focus, wrap the open in a transition so the current screen stays visible, and put a Suspense boundary with a skeleton close to the feature."
4 · Deep-dive "The boundaries that pay are large and rarely used. Small shared components pay negatively: extra requests for almost no saving."
5 · Failure modes "What goes wrong is spinner flashes on every interaction, nested lazy components loading in a waterfall, and splitting code the first paint needs."
6 · Evolve "I verify with a bundle analyser and a throttled network, and hold a size budget per route in CI."
Close "Split what the first screen doesn't need, and hide the wait you introduced."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: what is on the first screen
stages.html:
Code Where it goes
needed for the first paint of the route main chunk
the rest of this route, below the fold or behind a click lazy
other routes their own chunks
  • Everything needed for the initial route's first paint stays in the main chunk; everything else is a candidate.

stages.name: Constraints
stages.html:
Without splitting:all code up frontslow first loadinstant feature
With splitting:fast first loada request when the feature is first usedfeature
  • Each split point adds a request when first used; on slow networks that's visible.

stages.name: Baseline boundaries
stages.html:
Prove it — lazy + prefetch on intent + transition:

const loadEditor = () => import('./RichEditor')
const RichEditor = lazy(loadEditor)
function EditButton() {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false)
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition()
  return <>
    <button onMouseEnter={loadEditor} onFocus={loadEditor} onClick={() => startTransition(() => setOpen(true))}>
      {isPending ? 'Opening…' : 'Edit'}
    </button>
    {open && <Suspense fallback={<EditorSkeleton />}><RichEditor /></Suspense>}
  </>
}

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.html:
Boundary Payoff
routes biggest, automatic in frameworks
modals/editors/settings large, rarely used code
heavy libraries (charts, PDF, maps) large vendor chunks
small shared components negative: extra requests

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Failure Cause Guard
a spinner replaces half the page no transition; Suspense boundary too high a transition, and a boundary near the feature
chunks load one after another nested lazy components load siblings in parallel; prefetch
the same library in several chunks bundler configuration check the analyser for duplicates
worse LCP first-screen code was split keep it in the main chunk
  • Spinner flashes on every interaction; waterfalls of nested lazy chunks; duplicated vendor code across chunks; splitting first-screen code (worse LCP).

stages.name: Evolve
stages.claim: JS per route and a CI budget
stages.html:
Measure Tool
JavaScript per route a bundle analyser on the production build
LCP and INP field monitoring
time to open a split feature a throttled network profile
growth over time a per-route size budget in CI
  • JS per route (bundle analyzer), LCP and INP in the field, time-to-open for split features on a throttled network, and a CI bundle-size budget.

followUps.question: A lazy modal is opened with plain setOpen(true) (no transition) inside an existing Suspense boundary high up the tree. What does the user see?
followUps.html:
The nearest Suspense fallback shows, possibly replacing a large part of the page.

Opened with The user sees
plain setOpen(true) the fallback of the nearest boundary, until the chunk loads
a transition the current screen, then the modal

followUps.question: "Split every component for the smallest bundle."
followUps.html:
Tiny chunks add requests and waterfalls; total bytes barely change.

  • Split at meaningful boundaries: routes, click-to-open surfaces, heavy libraries.

followUps.question: How does Next.js App Router change this?
followUps.html:
Much of it becomes automatic.

  • Routes are split for you.
  • Server Components don't ship their code at all.
  • next/dynamic for heavy client-only components.
  • Links in the viewport are prefetched.

followUps.question: How do you find what to split?
followUps.html:
A bundle analyser on the production build.

analysefind large modules in the main chunkcheck whether the first screen uses themsplit the ones it doesn't

followUps.question: How do you keep bundles from growing back?
followUps.html:
With a budget and a habit.

  • A per-route size budget in CI that fails the build.
  • Review of every new heavy dependency.
  • A dashboard of JavaScript per route over time.

react-q33.testing: the Rules of Hooks and how React detects violations.
react-q33.trap: answering from the rule alone. Measured on React 19.3, this exact snippet doesn't throw — the drill's key (B) is wrong for it.
react-q33.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Predict it out loud "On React 19.3 this exact snippet renders Login without an error, and the name state is discarded. I checked it."
2 · Trace the render "The code does break the Rules of Hooks: the early return makes useState conditional, so the linter flags it. But React's runtime check compares hook counts between renders, and it only fires when at least one hook ran before the render stopped short. Here no hook runs before the return, so going from forty-two to null renders Login quietly, and when the user ID comes back the input starts empty."
3 · The rule that decides it "So the rule: hooks are matched by call order, and the too-few-hooks check needs a partly consumed list to notice."
4 · Variants that flip it "Add any hook above the early return and it does throw, rendered fewer hooks than expected, and rendered more hooks in the other direction."
5 · The production version "In production the quiet case is the worse one: user input vanishes with no error. So I rely on the hooks lint rule as an error in CI, not on the runtime."
Close "Hooks above every early return, or split the branch into its own component."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
function Profile({ userId }) {
  if (!userId) return <Login />;
  const [name, setName] = useState('');
  return <input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} />;
}
  • A: renders <Login /> fine, state is discarded · B: throws — "Rendered fewer hooks than expected" · C: name silently becomes undefined · D: React warns in dev, works in prod

stages.name: Trace the render
stages.html:
Prove it — four variants on React 19.3 (jsdom harness):

Variant Sequence Result
this snippet (no hook before return) "42" → null no error; renders login
this snippet null → "42" no error; renders input
this snippet, typed "typed" "42" → null → "42" input comes back empty (state discarded)
hook before the return "42" → null throws Rendered fewer hooks than expected…
hook before the return null → "42" throws Rendered more hooks than during the previous render.

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.claim: the check needs a partial list
stages.html:
Hooks called before the early return Runtime check Result
none nothing to compare renders; the component's hook state is cleared
one or more the count differs from the previous render throws
  • Hooks are matched by call order (Q7). React detects "too few" when the render stopped partway through the previous list; a render that calls zero hooks isn't caught, and the component's hook state is simply cleared.

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.claim: one hook above makes it throw
stages.html:
Fix A:all hooks firstthen if (!userId) return <Login />
Fix B:Profile chooses<ProfileForm /> or <Login />each has a fixed hook list
  • Any hook above the if → throws in both directions (table above).
  • Split: function Profile({ userId }) { return userId ? <ProfileForm /> : <Login /> } — each component has a fixed hook list; ProfileForm's state resets naturally when it unmounts.

stages.name: The production version
stages.claim: silent state loss, not a crash
stages.html:
Outcome Visible to the team? Visible to the user?
throws yes: an error in development and in monitoring an error screen
renders with state discarded no typed input is silently lost

The guard is eslint-plugin-react-hooks with rules-of-hooks as an error.

  • The non-throwing case loses user input silently. Rely on eslint-plugin-react-hooks (rules-of-hooks: error), not on runtime errors.

followUps.question: Add const theme = useContext(ThemeCtx) as the first line. Now what happens on "42" → null?
followUps.html:
It throws "Rendered fewer hooks than expected".

render 1: useContext, useStaterender 2: useContext, then returnone hook ran, two expectederror

followUps.question: "It always throws; that's what the rules of hooks are for."
followUps.html:
The runtime check doesn't catch every violation.

Guard Catches this snippet?
runtime check on React 19.3 no: it renders and drops state
the lint rule yes

followUps.question: Why does the zero-hook render slip through?
followUps.html:
With zero hooks called there is no partial list to compare.

  • The check fires when a render ends partway through the previous list.
  • A render with no hooks at all just resets the component's hook state.

followUps.question: What's the idiomatic fix?
followUps.html:
Hooks above the early return, or separate components.

Fix When
move hooks up the hooks are cheap and always valid
split into ProfileForm and Login each branch has its own state

followUps.question: What would you tell the team after finding this?
followUps.html:
That "the app didn't crash" is no evidence for hooks code.

  • rules-of-hooks as an error in CI.
  • No reliance on runtime errors or manual review.

dontSay: "It always throws" (not for this snippet on 19.3).

react-q34.testing: field data (RUM) over lab data, the right metrics, segmentation and guardrails.
react-q34.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "First I'd agree which routes and interactions matter: search, checkout, sending a chat message."
2 · Constraints "Then field data, not lab data. My laptop is fast, on a good network, with a warm cache. Users aren't."
3 · Baseline setup "The core is the web-vitals library in the app, sending Core Web Vitals to our analytics: INP for interaction responsiveness, which is where React re-render problems show up, LCP for loading, and CLS for layout stability."
4 · Deep-dive "I report them at the seventy-fifth percentile, segmented by route, device class and connection, because averages hide the slow devices where the problems live. INP attribution tells me which interaction and element was slow. For React-specific cost, the Profiler component's onRender callback can sample commit durations in production."
5 · Failure modes "The failure modes are measuring only in the lab, reporting averages, and dashboards nobody watches."
6 · Evolve "Lab tools stay as guards: Lighthouse CI and a bundle budget on every pull request, with alerts on p75 regressions per route after a deploy."
Close "Real users, the right three metrics, at p75, by route and device."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
Decide Example
key routes search, product page, checkout, chat
key interactions type in search, add to cart, send message
target a p75 threshold per metric, per route
devices that matter the mid-range phones your users really have
  • Key routes and interactions (search, checkout, chat send); target percentiles and devices.

stages.name: Constraints
stages.claim: real devices are slow and varied
stages.html:
Lab (Lighthouse, DevTools) Field (real-user monitoring)
Device and network yours your users'
Interactions scripted or none real
Good for catching regressions before release knowing what users experience
  • Mid-range Android on 4G is a very different world from a developer laptop; field data captures it.

stages.name: Baseline setup
stages.html:
Prove it — reporting INP with attribution:

import { onINP, onLCP, onCLS } from 'web-vitals/attribution'
function send(metric) {
  navigator.sendBeacon('/rum', JSON.stringify({
    name: metric.name, value: metric.value, route: location.pathname,
    target: metric.attribution?.interactionTarget, device: navigator.hardwareConcurrency,
  }))
}
onINP(send); onLCP(send); onCLS(send)

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.html:
Metric Measures "Good" threshold (Google)
INP interaction → next paint ≤ 200 ms
LCP largest content visible ≤ 2.5 s
CLS layout shifts ≤ 0.1
React <Profiler> commit time (sampled) render cost of subtrees your budget
  • Segment by route, device, network; report p75, not averages.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Failure Consequence
lab-only measurement a good score, slow users
averages the slow tail disappears
no segmentation one slow route or device class is hidden
Profiler on for every session overhead for all users
dashboards with no alerts regressions noticed weeks later
  • Lab-only measurement; averages; no segmentation; Profiler on for everyone (overhead); dashboards nobody watches.

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
Alert Fires on
INP or LCP p75 per route a regression after a deploy
bundle budget a pull request that exceeds it
long animation frames a spike in main-thread blocking
  • INP/LCP p75 regressions per route after deploys, bundle budget failures in CI, and long-animation-frame spikes.

followUps.question: 🧪 Lighthouse shows 98 on your laptop; field INP p75 is 450 ms. Which do you believe?
followUps.html:
The field data: it is real users.

Lighthouse 98 Field INP p75 450 ms
Measures a scripted load on your hardware real interactions on real devices

Use INP attribution to find the slow interactions.

followUps.question: "Lighthouse score is our performance metric."
followUps.html:
It is a synthetic lab score.

  • Good for CI guards.
  • Not a measure of how users experience the app.

followUps.question: Why p75?
followUps.html:
It reflects most users without being dominated by extreme outliers.

Statistic Problem
mean hides the slow tail
p99 noisy, dominated by outliers
p75 what the Core Web Vitals assessment uses

followUps.question: Is the React Profiler safe in production?
followUps.html:
Yes, sampled.

  • <Profiler> works in production builds; detailed timings need a profiling build.
  • It has overhead, so enable it for a small share of sessions.

followUps.question: For an AI chat app, what extra metric would you add?
followUps.html:
The metrics of a stream.

  • Time to first token, as seen in the browser.
  • Frames dropped while tokens render.
  • INP of the send action during a stream.

react-q35.testing: the user-visible effect: responsiveness under heavy renders, no jarring fallbacks.
react-q35.trap: "it makes rendering faster" or "it renders in parallel threads".
react-q35.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "Concurrent rendering makes rendering interruptible and prioritised. The user-visible win is that urgent updates stay responsive while expensive ones happen in the background."
2 · Mechanism "Updates get priorities. Typing into a search box stays smooth even though the results list re-renders heavily, because React can interrupt the heavy render to handle the keystroke, then resume. And a transition can keep the current screen visible instead of flashing a spinner while new content gets ready."
3 · Where it doesn't help "It doesn't help everywhere. It doesn't make any render faster, and it isn't parallel threads: it is the same JavaScript thread, interleaved. One huge synchronous computation inside a single component still blocks."
4 · How I've used it "It pays in search-as-you-type, tab switches and filtering large dashboards."
5 · Adjacent concept "And it is opt-in, through transitions, deferred values and Suspense."
Close "Urgent updates jump the queue; heavy renders yield."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html:
"Urgent updates jump the queue; heavy renders yield."

Before (synchronous) Concurrent
A heavy render in progress blocks input until it finishes can be interrupted by a keystroke
New screen not ready a spinner replaces the old one the old screen stays, with a pending hint
Threads one one: interleaved, not parallel

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
One keystroke during a heavy render:heavy render runningReact yieldskeystroke rendered (urgent)heavy render restarts with the new state
Piece Role
lanes a priority per update
yielding a transition render checks regularly whether to pause
discarding interrupted work is thrown away and redone with fresh state
  • Updates get priorities (lanes); transition renders check periodically whether to yield to the browser or to more urgent work; interrupted work is discarded and redone with fresh state.

stages.name: Where it doesn't help
stages.html:
Doesn't help Why
one huge synchronous computation in render can't be split mid-function
slow effects run outside the render phase
network latency still waiting
urgent updates that are heavy themselves they aren't deferred

Prove it — the opt-in:

const [query, setQuery] = useState('')
const deferred = useDeferredValue(query)       // urgent: input; background: results
return <><input value={query} onChange={e => setQuery(e.target.value)} /><Results q={deferred} /></>

stages.name: How I've used it
stages.html:
Use What stays responsive
search-as-you-type with heavy results the input
a tab switch that loads data the current tab, until the next is ready
filtering a large dashboard the filter controls
  • Search-as-you-type with heavy results, tab switches that keep the old tab until data arrives, filtering large dashboards.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html:
API Marks as non-urgent
useTransition a state update you own
useDeferredValue a value you receive
Suspense where a loading state may appear (Q36)
  • Transitions decide whether a suspended update shows a fallback or keeps the old UI (Q36).

followUps.question: A Results component takes 300 ms to render and isn't split into smaller components. Does useDeferredValue keep typing smooth?
followUps.html:
Partly at best: React yields between components, not inside one function.

Results is Typing
many small components stays smooth
one 300 ms function still blocked for 300 ms

Split the work, or reduce it.

followUps.question: "Concurrent React renders in parallel on multiple threads."
followUps.html:
It is single-threaded.

  • Concurrency here means interleaving and priorities.
  • Not parallelism.

followUps.question: Do I get it automatically?
followUps.html:
The renderer, yes; the behaviour, no.

Default
createRoot enables the concurrent renderer
an update urgent, unless marked with a transition or deferred value

followUps.question: What does "tearing" have to do with this?
followUps.html:
Interruptible rendering can read an external store at two different moments.

  • useSyncExternalStore keeps the tree consistent (Q21).

followUps.question: How does it help an AI chat UI?
followUps.html:
It keeps the composer and scrolling responsive while tokens stream.

  • Markdown and code highlighting of the transcript rendered as non-urgent.
  • The composer and scroll position stay urgent.

react-q36.testing: same idea, different handle — who owns the state update.
react-q36.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Both mark work as non-urgent so the current UI stays responsive. The difference is where I have a handle: on the update, or only on the value."
2 · Where useTransition wins "useTransition wraps the state update. I use it when I own the setter: navigation, tab switches, filters. It gives me isPending to show a subtle indicator while the old UI stays on screen, and in React 19 it can wrap async functions, which is the basis for Actions."
3 · Where useDeferredValue wins "useDeferredValue wraps a value. I use it when I only receive the value, a prop or state owned elsewhere, and want an expensive child to render with a lagging copy while the input stays urgent. Comparing the value with its deferred copy tells me the results are stale."
4 · The deciding question "So the question is simply whether I own the state update."
5 · What I'd pick "Transitions for tabs, navigation and filter changes; a deferred value for results downstream of an input. And neither is a debounce: they don't wait a fixed time, they render when there is capacity and discard outdated work."
Close "Wrap the update if you own it, wrap the value if you don't."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: wrap the update or wrap the value
stages.html:
useTransition useDeferredValue
you control the setter only the value
pending signal isPending value !== deferred
async (19) yes (Actions) —

stages.name: Where useTransition wins
stages.html:
Prove it — keep the old tab visible:

const [tab, setTab] = useState('about')
const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition()
<button onClick={() => startTransition(() => setTab('posts'))}>Posts{isPending && ' …'}</button>
<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}><TabPanel tab={tab} /></Suspense>
// if Posts suspends, the About panel stays visible instead of the Spinner

stages.name: Where useDeferredValue wins
stages.html:
function Results({ query }) {                        // query is a prop
  const deferred = useDeferredValue(query)
  const stale = query !== deferred
  return <div style={{ opacity: stale ? 0.6 : 1 }}><HeavyList q={deferred} /></div>
}

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: do you own the state update
stages.html:
Situation Use
I call the setter useTransition
the value arrives as a prop, or from a hook I don't control useDeferredValue
limiting network requests debounce, or a query library
  • Yes → useTransition. No → useDeferredValue.

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.html:
UI Pick
tabs, navigation, filter changes transition
a results list downstream of an input deferred value
a controlled input's own value neither: keep it urgent
  • Tabs, navigation, filter changes: transition. Search results downstream of an input: deferred value. Network requests: still debounce or use a query library.

followUps.question: You wrap setQuery for a controlled input in startTransition. What happens when typing?
followUps.html:
The input itself becomes non-urgent and feels sticky.

What is deferred Typing
the input's own value lags
only the expensive consumer smooth

followUps.question: "They're a built-in debounce."
followUps.html:
There is no fixed delay.

Debounce Transition or deferred value
Waits a fixed time until there is capacity
Outdated work still runs discarded

followUps.question: What does React 19 add to transitions?
followUps.html:
Async transitions.

startTransition(async () => { await save(); setX(…) }) ─▶ isPending covers the whole action

That is the basis of Actions and useActionState.

followUps.question: Do they help data fetching?
followUps.html:
They change what is shown while waiting, not how long the fetch takes.

  • With Suspense-enabled data they keep content on screen instead of a fallback.

followUps.question: Where in an AI app?
followUps.html:
In two places.

Interaction Tool
switching conversations a transition keeps the current one visible until the next loads
heavy markdown in a streaming message a deferred value, so scrolling stays smooth

dontSay: Picking by preference, not by who owns the update.

react-q37.testing: the RSC payload vs code, the client boundary, and serialisation rules.
react-q37.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "A Server Component runs only on the server, at build time or per request, and its code never ships to the browser. What ships is its output."
2 · What ships "That output is a serialised description of the rendered tree, the RSC payload, with placeholders where Client Components go, plus the JavaScript for those Client Components only. So server-only code, a markdown parser or a database client, adds nothing to the client bundle, and the component can be async and await the database directly."
3 · Prove it "The example shows it: the page reads posts and renders markdown on the server, and only the like button ships JavaScript."
4 · What you can't do "What I can't do follows from the fact that it has already finished running on the server: no state, no effects, no event handlers, no browser APIs. Anything interactive goes in a Client Component marked use client, and everything that file imports is client code. Props crossing the boundary must be serialisable."
5 · So what for the system "So I keep client boundaries small and low in the tree, pass plain data, and never pass secrets across. And it isn't SSR: SSR produces HTML for the first load; RSC decides which components ever run on the client."
Close "Output ships, code doesn't, and the use client line is the boundary."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html: "Server Components send a serialised render result, not their JavaScript; only Client Components ship code."

stages.name: What ships
stages.claim: a payload plus client component code
stages.html:
Item Ships to browser?
Server Component code and its imports no
RSC payload (rendered tree, props for client components) yes
Client Component code ('use client' and its imports) yes
HTML for first load (via SSR) yes

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
// app/posts/page.jsx — Server Component (default in App Router)
import { db } from '@/lib/db'                 // never bundled for the client
import { marked } from 'marked'               // never bundled for the client
import LikeButton from './LikeButton'         // 'use client' inside
export default async function Posts() {
  const posts = await db.post.findMany()
  return posts.map(p => (
    <article key={p.id}>
      <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: marked(p.body) }} />
      <LikeButton postId={p.id} />                {/* only this ships JS */}
    </article>
  ))
}
// LikeButton.jsx
'use client'
export default function LikeButton({ postId }) { const [liked, setLiked] = useState(false); return <button onClick={() => setLiked(!liked)}>♥</button> }

stages.name: What you can't do
stages.html:
Not in a Server Component Why
useState, useEffect, event handlers it doesn't run in the browser
browser APIs (window, localStorage) no browser on the server
useContext no client React tree there
passing functions as props to client components not serialisable (Server Actions excepted)

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
Practice Why
'use client' on interactive leaves, not on layouts everything a client file imports becomes client code
serialisable props across the boundary functions and class instances can't cross (Server Actions excepted)
select only the fields the client needs every prop is visible in the payload
fetch in Server Components, in parallel no client waterfall, no UI-only endpoint
  • Keep 'use client' boundaries low and small (leaves), pass serialisable data, fetch in Server Components in parallel, and be careful with secrets — anything passed to a Client Component is visible in the browser.

followUps.question: You put 'use client' at the top of the root layout. What happens to the app?
followUps.html:
Everything imported below becomes client code.

'use client' placed on Effect
the root layout the whole tree ships and hydrates: the benefits are gone
interactive leaves only those ship JavaScript

followUps.question: "RSC is just SSR."
followUps.html:
They answer different questions.

SSR RSC
Produces HTML for the first load a payload of rendered output
Component code ships and hydrates yes no
Used together yes, in Next.js yes

followUps.question: Can a Client Component render a Server Component?
followUps.html:
Not by importing it, but it can receive one as children.

Server Componentrenders <ClientShell><ServerPart /></ClientShell>ServerPart is rendered on the server and passed in as a prop

followUps.question: What's a security risk with RSC?
followUps.html:
Leaking data through props.

  • Passing a whole user record or a token to a Client Component serialises it into the payload.
  • Select only what the client needs, on the server.

followUps.question: How would you use RSC in an AI product?
followUps.html:
Server Components for reading, Client Components for interacting.

Part Kind
conversation list and history Server Components, close to the data
composer and streaming view Client Components
the call to the model on the server, so keys stay there

dontSay: 'use client' at the root by default.
